00005051ae673b8d6a65d137e0bf6bb11864938a.en:
If your life is spent high up in the blue skies, what happens when you’re forced to come back down to earth with a bump? ‘Down to Earth’ blends the personal and the political in the story of an ambitious F-16 fighter pilot whose career in the skies comes to a premature end when she is posted to a drone control base. This compelling narrative powerfully tackles the most pressing contemporary issues with irony and conviction! It explores questions of war, family and the courage to stand up to a system that brooks no opposition.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

0116afcf398f1e68548bd2416c9e23f26a80f7ad.en:
If you think that life as an adult is hard, just think back to what it was like when you were sixteen. Those are years that many people overlook, yet they actually turn out to be crucial in shaping a person. That’s when you face your first problems – at first glance, insurmountable, crushing, devastating, yet they actually turn out to be crucial moments that shape you. These are also the carefree years – secret parties, secret boyfriends or girlfriends, that first drag on a cigarette, getting drunk for the first time, and, of course, the thrill of your parents having no idea what’s going on. One of the most beautiful feelings is first love. Falling in love at that age is something that never happens again in quite the same way – raw, painful, genuine. Your body throbs at unpredictable frequencies, your mind refuses to think rationally, and your heart doesn’t want to know about the consequences. For some, this is also when ‘the first time’ happens – an event that is either huge, almost supernatural – or simply something that has to happen, just like that.

The play ‘THE TRUTH OR DARE’ pits a boy and a girl against each other in a duel, disguised as a game in which there are no rules – only impulses, laughter, insults and secrets they aren’t ready to admit even to themselves. Because at sixteen, life is either a drama or a comedy – and most often both at once. And sometimes it all starts with a simple question: Truth… or dare?

0301eb6b5eb3a41fdd4455403a609dc2dc584c93.en:
There are weeks when the only thing that gives them meaning is the anticipation of Friday night. There are days spent entirely planning for it. There are people for whom Friday night is like a religious festival.

But there are also quite a few who can only celebrate it in their wildest dreams. Take the ‘dads’, for example. Four young men, who find themselves with fewer and fewer opportunities to let their hair down, tell us how a Friday night might unfold as they slip into different roles. They show us which is the right key and which is the right door, and then demonstrate how a Friday night bender can throw the whole puzzle into disarray. They lead us towards a dream ending to the evening, but a trip to the loo suddenly changes everything.

0444f55618c71058c658091eedbccb2963b90876.en:
A confirmed bachelor is browsing the marriage adverts because, 12 years ago, he promised his mother he would get married. Suddenly, he comes across something very intriguing: ‘A young, beautiful, wealthy and well-off woman is looking for an ugly and poor man to make him happy’. And so, he decides to get to know her. Perhaps because, as he thinks, his chances of success are very slim. It becomes clear that someone had advised the beauty, who until then had lived solely for her own pleasure, to do at least one good deed for another person – to make him happy.

And so begins the story of how a man, left behind on the home front of love, becomes a victor. The beauty falls in love with a beast, and instead of turning into a prince, he becomes a real beast – arrogant, fussy and demanding. Because happiness, as the protagonist (and the audience) realise, is a very great trial for a weak person.

The play *The Different One* is described by its author, Alexei Slapovsky, as a ‘comic tragedy’ – a genre as contemporary as it is challenging. What in this story is true and what is fiction? Which of the characters is genuine and which is ‘different’? And is ‘The Different One’ really different?

Among his twelve commandments, the playwright Alexei Slapovsky places the following at the top of the list:

1. Love not the theatre that already exists, but the theatre that is yet to come.

2. Treat playwriting as you would literature.

North Macedonia. The public debate on both sides of the border is always emotional and often touches on sensitive issues that spark ongoing disputes. How does all this affect our everyday interactions, our friendships,

our professional contacts, our creative collaborations – indeed, our relationships as people and neighbours? These are just some of the seemingly simple questions that the production team ask themselves and seek to discuss with the audience. Yet they provoke

Nowhere do they teach you how to live. There are universities, psychotherapists, churches, psychoanalysts, pseudo-occult teachers, all manner of spiritual practices and meditations, but it seems nowhere do they get to the heart of the matter. There is hardly a single person who has come to terms with themselves and the meaning of their own existence. ‘I don’t know any happy people,’ as Chekhov says.

‘Fear of Taming’ tells, with understanding and a sense of humour, the story of four people trying to understand the reasons and causes of their failures in life, to express their hatreds and loves, but also to see the meaning of a second chance in every person’s life. And why not make us reflect on the quiet yet powerful wisdom of goodness and humanity, as well as on a possible way out of the ‘fear of taming’ – that is, of getting used to or adapting to it and its consequences. Or, as one of the characters says: ‘Just say something nice and let’s get on with it!’

0c929c2e13da8b88e97b65d9f4ffa0af7a008455.en: The 1990s in Ukraine were a time of instability, material deprivation and complex relationships between parents and children. Against this backdrop unfolds the touching friendship between little Timofey, a sensitive boy who grew up without a father’s care, and Felix – his grandmother’s eccentric friend, a veteran of the war in Afghanistan. Felix suffers from post-traumatic stress and finds solace in music and alcohol. ‘Rock. Paper. Hand grenade’ is a raw, yet tender and heart-warming coming-of-age story about the first lessons in kindness and cruelty, teenage love, and the role of family and friends in the unstable environment of post-Soviet Ukraine. Irina Tsilik’s feature film debut is a moving coming-of-age drama set against the backdrop of the 1990s. (And of an inscrutable future that turned out to be harsher and darker.) Irina co-wrote the screenplay for *Stone. Paper. Grenade* with her husband Artem Chekh, author of the novel *Who Are You?*. Chekh is currently serving in the Ukrainian army. His book, which inspired the film, is a biography of a real-life figure of whom he has fond memories. The film’s wonderfully melancholic pace is down to the director’s masterful handling of sound and music. Every scene is carefully thought out and calibrated. Three different actors – Andriy Cherednyk, Vladyslav Balyuk and Volodymyr Hladkyi – take on the role of Tymofii at different ages. The role of his mother is played by the talented Anastasia Karpenko, known for her brilliant performance in the film *How Is Katya?*. Ukrainian director and journalist Iryna Tsilik made a name for herself with the documentary *The Earth Is Blue Like an Orange* (2020), which won the competition at Sundance in 2020; and was selected for the Berlinale, IDFA and more than 100 other international festivals.

0d79f9abaadcf990a574609a8c171c4f59f68e29.en:
In his book *On Liberty*, Timothy Snyder identifies factuality as one of the key characteristics of the most fundamental human value. Facts are the foundation of freedom. Without them, people would find it difficult to make informed choices or to recognise the manipulations of those in power and the status quo.

*‘My Name Was’* presents the stories of four women who survived the Revival Process. Each of them has her own autonomy and the right to be heard. Without confronting or contradicting one another, they provide the viewer with space to reflect on their own critical perspective and where it intersects with theirs.

0df56c086a10ad225eda4a48dd0d6f0e07ee9bd2.en:
The members of a scattered family are reunited on the threshold between life and death, on the borderline between reality and delirium, to tell one another everything they have kept silent about over the years. And to try to seek and grant forgiveness. Now, for the first time, they voice painful secrets, cruel truths and raw memories. They are all survivors. They have found a way to pick themselves up and carry on after the brutal twists and turns of life that have left them scarred for life. But the time has come to take stock. And once again they revisit their darkest sins, their unfulfilled loves and their unhealed emotional wounds, in the hope of finding HOPE.

The play is based on Yordan Slaveykov’s debut novel *The Last Step*, published by Janet 45 and reprinted several times. It was awarded the ‘Silver Pegasus’ for best novel in the prose category at the ‘Southern Spring’ competition, Haskovo, 2016, as well as the ‘Pencho’s Oak’ award, presented by Prof. Svetlozar Igov. It has also been nominated for the ‘Peroto’ Literary Club Award, National Palace of Culture.

In 2025, *The Last Step* is due to be published in German by Mauke and in Spanish by La tortuga Búlgara. Yordan Slaveykov is represented by the Sofia Literary Agency.

0e7e7fe0410bda9125c1c9a07d8e523e3efa5536.en:
Welcome to the BULGARIAN LESSON, in which artists from the ‘BULGARIAN ARMY’ Theatre company will be taking part.

We shall not simply repeat what is written in textbooks and volumes of literature about the life and work of Ivan Vazov, the Patriarch of Bulgarian literature, but we shall endeavour, through the medium of the spoken and performing arts (or the so-called ‘artistic word’), to explore a dozen of his timeless works.

The term ‘artistic word’ has a dual meaning: the author’s word is artistic, that is, the written word (in our case, this is indisputable and constitutes an eternal classic). It could also refer to the words of the performer who delivers them, that is, the living, spoken word.

0ebd232593c2f83484d33dac8d7a195af5ba9b98.en: In post-war Japan, a period marked by rapid economic growth, Kikuo Tachibana was born into a yakuza family. Following his father’s death, fate leads him to Hanjiro, a renowned Kabuki actor, who takes him under his wing. Kikuo discovers his calling and his talent as an actor blossoms. He meets Hanjiro’s son, Shunsuke, who becomes both his friend and his rival on stage. Nominated for an Oscar for Best Make-up and Hairstyling, this adaptation of the novel of the same name by Yoshida Shuichi went on to become the highest-grossing Japanese feature film in the history of the Japanese box office! Kokuhō literally means ‘national treasure’. 10bb09ca11013e1437d2816ed2ac0af12d5ae3c8.en:
The play “Quartet for Two” offers a brilliant, incisive and moving insight into human relationships.

It explores the relationship between a man and a woman, and the many facets of love! No one will remain unmoved by this humour-filled play by the Ukrainian master Anatoly Krym, at the heart of which lies the composer Yevgeny Alexandrovich! The day of his sixtieth birthday will prove to be the grand climax not only in his creative life, but also in his emotional world.

The duo – a married couple with 25 years of marital tolerance – gradually expands into a trio (the mistress whom the husband brings into their home to live alongside them), and then becomes a quartet (with the wife’s new lover). From a comedy of the ‘darling, I’ve fallen in love with another woman, but… I have absolutely no intention of moving out of the flat’ variety, through a series of comic situations featuring the wife’s relatively clever acts of revenge, to a tragicomedy in the finale – everyone falls into their own trap, because ‘25 years of one’s life, even if the emotions are different, cannot be torn off like a page from a calendar’. And the director cleverly sketches out today’s Salieri in action.

10bc077ec341c0f3684842eda5581a41f552a685.en:
If there is anything stronger than time, it is love. In *Constellations*, a man seeks a path to his lost beloved – beyond reality, into a dimension where memories and feelings create new worlds.

How long does life last, and how far does it extend? Is it possible for it to exist beyond its own end? What does ‘time’ mean in the context of the deterministic assumption that the end and the beginning are one and the same thing? Are the choices we make and stand by every day a manifestation of free will? Presumably so, if love and memories are capable of transporting us to another dimension, where we can forgive ourselves for our mistakes, reconsider our situations and destinies, overcome the pain, and perceive the multidimensional nature of what it means to be together.

‘Constellations’ is a mysterious play for two that takes us far into the realm of self-discovery. Nencho Kostov and Radina Dumanyan take on the complex, ambitious and rewarding roles of Roland and Merian.

10ce07a185fc50d2bc8f2bbbb20f8f727ecbbf97.en:
We don’t know what fate has in store for us, but we do know that in the show “Happy Together – Unhappy Together”, three women have got together to cook. Literally. And whatever they cook, they’ll serve it to the audience. Literally.

But can these three women actually cook? Who are they, anyway, that they’re going to be cooking? They’re stars of the dance world – both classical and contemporary. So why are they cooking rather than dancing? Hang on – nobody’s said they won’t be dancing whilst they cook. We’re just saying that in the end there’ll be a meal – we don’t know whether you’ll like the show or not, we don’t know whether you’ll be Happy or Unhappy, but you certainly won’t be leaving empty-handed.

But is that art? Look, precisely because it’s not certain what art is, we’re offering you something certain – something baked in the oven. And you’ll like it. As for the rest – who knows… In any case, Marta, Mila and Teodora will give it their all.

She is a psychotherapist; he is a lawyer. They are a couple who are as much in love as they are superstitious. One evening, they vow to remain faithful to one another for ten years, for the sake of their children.

Time passes and the end of this ‘period of fidelity’ draws near. And with it comes the moment of truth – how hard is it to say ‘I swear’?

12a2f0870e068ec6b2a0caff2eab3df0cbf8b183.en:
Ben Jonson’s *Volpone* (or *The Fox*) depicts a world in which wealth becomes the sole measure of value, and morality is readily traded for profit. Written over 400 years ago, the play feels remarkably contemporary because it speaks of something that time has failed to change – human greed.

The wealthy Venetian Volpone, aided by his cunning servant Mosca, pretends to be mortally ill in order to gather around him a whole crowd of ‘friends’ hoping to inherit his fortune. One after another, they bring gifts, flattery and promises, ready to stoop to any humiliation in the name of future gain.

As the story unfolds, the comedy becomes a sharply satirical mirror of human weaknesses – hypocrisy, self-interest and self-deception. Laughter comes easily, but it leaves us with the uncomfortable question of how much the characters on stage differ from ourselves.
12a2f0870e068ec6b2a0caff2eab3df0cbf8b183.src: „Волпоне“(или „Лисицата“) от Бен Джонсън рисува свят, в койт

12fd09ab4bdca19d2dfdf51653597362400cb369.en:
Alice is fifteen, a Year 9 pupil, with top marks in maths, English and history. She never forgets to sort her rubbish.

Ben is thirty-five, a marketing assistant. His interests include the gym, restaurants, vintage stuff and mojitos.

Charlie is twenty-five, unemployed, and has a bachelor’s degree in psychology. She lives in a house with four strangers and loves animation and 70s disco.

What connects the three of them is social isolation and a lack of genuine human connection. In a world where consumerism has reached its peak, status is defined by the things you own, friendship is measured in ‘likes’, and the future looks terrifying, they sometimes feel as though they don’t really exist. In an online world where every conversation is a potential commercial transaction, Alice, Ben and Charlie are increasingly losing their ability to be human.

And with a final effort, through extreme gestures that are both unsettling and surreal, they try to make sense of their lives.

Billy Collins’s play is dynamic, witty, ironic and unsparing in its analysis of consumer culture. As intended by the author, it is written to be performed by a single actor or actress and a drummer.

‘Over the Top’ tells unexpected stories in an unexpected way.

139cb4df4feed6c33e80d72f766f68b392deb5e2.en: Jumbo is a kind and sensitive boy who is often the target of teasing. He dreams of one day standing up to those who bully him and proving that he is not weak. But his life changes when he unexpectedly meets Mary – a mysterious little spirit from a magical world who needs help. Her family is in danger, and Jumbo must help her save her parents. Together with his best friends, he embarks on an incredible adventure in which the line between reality and the magical world blurs. Along the way, they encounter mysteries, funny moments, dangers and unexpected friendships. As he faces his fears and challenges, Jumbo gradually realises that true strength does not lie in being the bravest or the strongest, but in the ability to believe in oneself, to protect one’s friends and never to give up on those one loves.

13ea7a092f2be9a8ebe2281770d84d8a4518bdcd.en:
In this play, love is not a source of comfort, but a force that consumes. It is the fire that drives the characters forward, even when their path leads to their doom.

‘THE THESSALONIKI ASSASSINS’ introduces us to a group of young men driven by boundless love. They are prepared to do anything to change the fate of their people, realising that freedom is unthinkable without self-sacrifice. Nevertheless, they press on, driven not only by idealism but also by a deep, selfless love.

The play draws the audience into a world where love for a cause transcends personal fates and choices. Here, heroism is not merely an external feat, but also an internal struggle – a clash between fear and duty, life and self-sacrifice. Every gesture, every word on stage carries the weight of the inevitable, whilst emotion reaches its peak.

‘THE THESSALONIKI ASSASSINS’ inspires awe for the human will and reminds us that freedom always comes at a price – and that it can only be paid by those who truly love.

148f81a57eda479b42d6f479a7ede12fed3ac333.en: ‘The Sea After You’ is a story about two people and an imaginary friend – or, to be more precise, a play for two instruments and an inner voice. This text is like an emotional map of deeply hidden, personal territories, for which we spend our whole lives waiting to meet someone with whom to share them. It explores the nuances of feelings and the inspiration drawn from living – things that cannot be seen or touched. For anyone who has a complex relationship with life, inspiration is a precious and hard-to-find drug. When you do find it, however, you become a composer who has found a piano on a desert island. My characters meet on a ‘desert island’ and, thanks to the magnificent Radena Vulkanova, Julian Vergov and Petar Antonov, and Mariy Rosen’s direction, I am currently standing in silence, listening to their music. And our shared island is no longer deserted.

14b28d24edfa357d8ba95f5416854000e7cb08cf.en:
Does everything around you seem gloomy and monotonous?

Are you fed up with having pointless conversations?

Here’s the solution to all your problems!

THE TELEVISION!!!

Just an arm’s length away!

With just one click of a button, your life will change, carefree days will reign, and your happiness is guaranteed! Right now, at the lowest possible price, you’ll have the chance to settle comfortably on the sofa and a smile will instantly light up your face!

Tune in to the most absurd evening, where the telly becomes the third member of the family, and reality and illusion collide with such force that the sofa springs will creak for a very long time.

This is a tragic farce in which laughter erupts where you least expect it, and the truth is so absurd that it sounds like fiction. Words fly like slaps, love drowns in adverts, and stars die on television – but always with a generous dose of glamour.

‘PRIVATE SCREENING’ is a show that won’t let you doze off on the sofa, but grabs you and throws you straight into the eye of the storm. Where the remote control is a weapon, the heart is the target, and chaos dictates the rules. It is here that laughter and tears intertwine in a frenzied dance, where tenderness collides head-on with hysteria, and love seems both madly funny and terribly tragic.

154e6b1728e8324d1a5a02a847a54a40ad86538f.en:
‘Art’ is a moving story about art, friendship and our ability to remain true to ourselves, but also to our friends, when we see the world in a different way.

How much would you pay for a white painting? Does it matter who the artist is? Can we call a painting ‘art’ if all we see before us is a white canvas?

Serge (Petar Petrov – Pero) buys a painting for an exorbitant sum. It consists of a large canvas, painted white, with ‘fine white diagonal stripes’. To one of his best friends – Mark (Georgi Gotzin) – the painting is ‘rubbish’ and Serge has lost his mind. Their mutual best friend, Ivan (Kiril Nedkov), finds himself in the awkward position of having to navigate between the two, even though he himself is bogged down in countless personal problems related to the preparations for his wedding.

Can a single painting put long-standing friendships to the test? The arguments ‘for’ and ‘against’ the painting cross the line of good taste. The three best friends use it as a pretext to say what they really think of one another, and their friendships seem increasingly fragile and a source of weariness rather than inspiration.

Will Serge, Mark and Ivan manage to preserve their 15-year friendship, or will a single painting bring it to an end?

15a5dbcde24b2e4d15fe73c7e01efad0809ee73e.en:
On 9 December, HaHaHa Impro is celebrating 17 years since its first live show; to mark the occasion, we’ve put together a unique performance, taking place for the third time at Toplocentral. It will feature two stages, three cameras, 28 spotlights, over 5 actors, the same director, 2 musicians, a cake (if you bring one), 3 kg of roasted chestnuts, 3 bags of popcorn, 16 kg of emotional baggage and more.

Bulgaria’s most experienced improv actors, led by Ivaylo Rogozinov. A show in the style of HaHaHa, in which the actors will perform both standing and lying down (injuries are possible); it’s quite possible that some of them won’t be able to stand up again. Come and witness a show not seen for two years (the show may contain traces of peanuts and other nuts; no high gluten content is expected).

The long-form format presents a single story on stage throughout the entire show. The characters, the setting, the characters’ objectives and all the details are drawn from the audience. The challenge for the actors in the long-form format lies precisely in the development of the character, their story and their progression or decline. In this particular case, the story will unfold across two separate realities and two different perspectives (from the front and from above).

15c1e8ca4f75dba571c04f55d644f2bd948c5491.en:
In a world where everyone is searching for love, recognition and the meaning of their own existence, the characters in *The Seagull* find themselves prisoners of their dreams, fears and unrequited feelings.

A boy and a girl are in love. They dream of fame, glamour and happiness. He wants to become a great writer; she, a famous actress. Their desire is to escape the quagmire of provincial life. With the arrival of the boy’s mother – a famous actress – and her friend – a great writer, who possess everything the young couple aspire to, everything changes in an instant. The girl falls in love with the successful writer, who can quickly launch her on the path to fame.

‘The Seagull’ is a play about love that fails to find its way, about art that demands sacrifice, and about the person who continues to search for their place in the world.

174531ed01c7ff07973ef253bb906e723ca50282.en:
How might we describe Maria Virkhov? Many readers would probably say that she is the most iconic Bulgarian underground poet of the last thirty years, and perhaps of all time. Virhov is indeed a unique phenomenon – torn between the influences of Bulgarian and Russian poetry, but also that of punk. Leading the life of an outsider – some might say almost a vagrant’s existence – yet also translating poetry from foreign languages. Consuming books and alcohol, films and drugs in equal measure. Found dead in the Perlovo River.

This journey through her poetry is the work of a young and talented team, led by director Rostislav Georgiev, who recently received the ‘Askeer’ Award for Best Debut. Their exploration of Virhov’s work will help viewers glimpse the underground realms of Virhov’s soul, whilst also enabling readers familiar with her poetry to see her in a new light.

17af1af29ab33fefaa5599be1b06a55f56e529d5.en:
The whisky’s flowing, the truths are coming to light, and the rain won’t stop.

What do you get when you put four women, a steam cleaner and a stolen idea together? Answer: total chaos and egos soaked to the bone!

‘Code Yellow’ is a comedy that asks the question: Can the women’s revolution happen without someone having to clean up afterwards?

Niki, a talented young architect on the verge of completing her first solo project, is getting ready for an important dinner with her boss. But instead, her neighbour Emma turns up at her door – armed with feminist slogans and the unsettling ability to turn any conversation into a lecture on patriarchy. Whilst Niki tries to get her to leave, her boss cancels the meeting on the pretext of having ‘stomach trouble’.

After three glasses of whisky and a host of conspiracy theories, Niki and Emma sneak into the architectural firm to look for ‘clues’. But they aren’t the only ones with this idea. There they find Adriana – the boss’s elegant wife – who is looking for a slightly different sort of compromising evidence against her husband!

As the rain falls harder and harder, flooding the basements, the tension in the office mounts, and the evening turns into a comical confrontation when the cleaner, Blagovesta, joins the group.

The four women turn out to be far more involved with the boss than they ever imagined.

And so, four women, each completely different from the other, armed with a bottle of whisky and a steam cleaner, embark on a night full of comical situations, in which, driven by their feminist rebellion, they organise a fun and chaotic plan for revenge.

19789df9ace4a09c6ac6158c6bfbeeebb522deef.en:
Marriage offers no promise of happiness, but freedom threatens them with social failure, branded with the label ‘old bachelors and old maids’.

With the intelligence and hesitations of Hamlet, our hero stands on the cusp between self-contempt and arrogance, forced to choose between two women he cannot stand. He must choose between elusive heroism and the horror of living the life of an average loser. Yet standing in his way are two dangerously clever ladies, and two masterful seducers – pick-up artists. And so, five people find themselves pitted against one another with the aim of getting married, without wanting to.

Hanoh Levin follows in the footsteps of Gogol and Molière, except that from these ‘categorised’ characters emerge real people with their candid, unvarnished and unsentimental strategy for sexual survival.

Love is bittersweet among the poets of love; Hanoch Levin’s laughter is bittersweet on the flip side of love.

On 24 November, Toplocentral turns 5! We’ll be marking the anniversary with a whole week of celebrations and a specially curated programme.

Toplocentrala evolves with every new artistic idea, with the people who bring it to life, and with the issues of our time. Over these five years, our spaces have hosted various art forms, provided a space for experimentation, and brought artists and audiences together in a shared experience.

For the celebrations, we have selected events that turn this gathering into a true sensory adventure — an opportunity to discover new artistic approaches, broaden your horizons and share the celebrations with us.

The programme also includes an ‘Open Day’ on 22 November. We invite you to explore Toplocentral’s spaces and get to know them up close. For those who haven’t visited us yet, this is a great opportunity for a first visit.

Take a look at our November programme and choose the events that excite you. We look forward to welcoming you so we can celebrate this occasion together.

Whether it is an ancient fire cult or a ritual for divination, whether it is accepted or condemned by the Church, it makes no difference to art. Fire-walking is an integral part of Bulgaria’s heritage. The power of purification – this is what inspires the artists of the Burgas Puppet Theatre as they draw upon this unique, centuries-old Bulgarian tradition. This modern, large-scale and powerful visual and physical performance draws us back to ourselves, to the connection with our souls, and carries a message of collective purification for the society in which we live.

The characters experience unpredictable moments of love and loss, unexpected encounters and partings that will restore your faith in romantic destiny and the wild logic of the heart. Matteo meets Greta in Rome. He is playing tennis when she, on her way to her own wedding, stops for a set with him, a complete stranger. After thrashing him, she dashes off to get married with a beaming smile. Not only has he been defeated on the court, but Mateo is already in love – yet what can he do? Years later, in San Sebastián, their paths cross once more. Mateo is at a Bruce Springsteen concert when he spots Greta searching for her missing daughter. He then sees her again by chance in a Roman café. She is still with her husband, and Mateo has recently got married… Inspired by the stories of Eshkol Nevo, *It Will Happen Tonight* celebrates those moments when the universe seems to knock on the door with a wink, hinting at another possible life.

1ad444bc0bbfb6572e89e2a36d101852fbe3472c.en:
Described as a theatrical magician, a controversial avant-gardist, hailed as a pioneer in theatrical language and work with actors… Ivan Stanev described himself as a ‘belated modernist’. Throughout his creative career, he found himself caught between ‘hosanna’ and ‘crucify him’ whenever he presented his latest theatrical or visual provocation to audiences and critics alike. Ivan’s first return to Bulgaria following his emigration to Germany in 1988 was a guest performance of his original play *Performance and Punishment* –

a production created in 1990 as a co-production between the Hebbel Theatre in Berlin, the ‘Theater der Welt’ festival in Essen and ‘Eurokaz’ in Zagreb. The production was met with rapturous applause from theatre audiences across Europe and in Sofia.

“PERFORMANCE AND PUNISHMENT” is transgressive to the point of brutality – a “reprise” on Dostoevsky’s novel.

Stanev delights in dissecting and reinventing the language of theatre. He skilfully manipulates and sets fire to traditional stage conventions. The author combines a lofty style of expression with jokes that are sardonic to the point of cynicism. He ironically juggles the categories of Guilt, Repentance and Truth – long since buried in the inner filth like dirty, shameful underwear. With incredibly gentle tones, he marks the death not only of the individual, but also of the public spirit. A world derailed by false propriety and self-satisfied ‘etiquette’ – concealing the dishonour and atrocities with which we have resigned ourselves to living.

‘PERFORMANCE AND PUNISHMENT’ is an exceptional text written ‘without hope or despair’.

1b630e52d358b70501c468cff136b4c7e04aa396.en:
The vexing question of why all ideas fail when put into practice has no expiry date. It continues to weigh heavily on the mind to this day and has given rise to many attempts to find an answer, some of which are downright grotesque. It is unbelievable that in the 21st century, prominent figures are insisting on the return of public capital punishment. That the guillotine should be brought back.

The maxim ‘love thy neighbour as thyself’ is the most beautiful answer possible. But it is also the most daunting. It is no coincidence that it is not among the Ten Commandments of the Old Testament – you cannot love by command. Nor is it a New Testament sermon.

‘Love your neighbour’ is Christ’s cry for salvation, hard-won by himself; his realisation that love is the only possible antidote to evil, ruin and destruction.

The spirit standing up to the devil – the only possible conspiracy in the name of good.

Alas, Prince Myshkin’s Don Quixote-like efforts to save his fallen neighbour—not through advice and instruction, but by taking on his suffering in the hope that the archetype might be revealed through his darkened countenance—fail. For the prince, there is You; for the other, there is only I.

But the power of his suicidal gesture (‘What are you doing to yourself, Prince?’) lies in this: at least for a moment, at least whilst they are together – to awaken in his neighbour the memory of the light, to enlighten him.
1b630e52d358b70501c468cff136b4c7e04aa396.src: Проклетият въпрос защо всичките идеи се провалят в човешкото

1b7b064304aebef41f93cb430ac6283f1a20bf7c.en:
Published in 1925, four years before the catastrophic crash of the American stock markets and the onset of the Great Depression, F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel depicts a society being torn apart by money, greed and insatiability. The American dream of happiness and individualism, the pursuit of wealth and glamour at any cost. Where do they end? Can one ever attain them, or are they merely a fantasy that remains solely in the longing for utopian happiness? Can we hold on to our dreams and recognise beauty, love and loneliness when we encounter them in the sea of chaos around us?

The performance will also explore the myths surrounding dreams. Dreams that inspire. Dreams that destroy. Dreams that turn into bittersweet memories.

1c7b04fb79b477d3849c425f8c88458dd49e55df.en:
Longings, discord, friendship and betrayal, love and indifference…

People feigning feelings and warmth…

Who hasn’t been disappointed by all this?

*The Misanthrope* is one of the best-known and most frequently staged comedies by the great French playwright Jean-Baptiste Molière. The play was first performed on 4 June 1666 at the Palais-Royal in Paris. Molière himself played the lead role. The troupe performed 34 consecutive shows, and by the end of Louis XIV’s reign, the play had been staged 199 times. This fact clearly demonstrates that, even upon its debut, Molière’s sombre *The Misanthrope* touched upon important issues of the time, human nature and morality.

The play *The Misanthrope* deals with relationships and situations in which we have all found ourselves and suffered setbacks. It exposes self-love, flattery and duplicity with such brilliance and passion that, over the years, it has garnered exceptional acclaim and fame, and today it feels more relevant than ever.

The protagonist, Alceste, has become one of the most complex and appealing roles for actors in classical theatre. He is the most serious, the most noble, the most exalted comic character, in whom the comic intersects with courage and virtue.

1f0786b03bc231ce0e69ed9592a156624ff5ce48.en:
“There Were Ten” transports the audience into an atmosphere of tension and mystery, where ten people, linked by secrets from the past, find themselves stranded on an island. Each of them has reason to be afraid, as an unknown killer begins to prey on the guests, following the tune of a sinister nursery rhyme.

The marvellous writer, Agatha Christie, told us that she came up with the plots for her novels whilst washing up. It was such a mindless task that thoughts of murder would inevitably pop into her head. After her confession, whilst stroking my cat (another silly pastime), I read this play of hers. Wow! She’s very clever. Although it’s a madly criminal story. Evil is in it, but… there’s also heavenly love. Good triumphs over evil! But who are the bad guys? Oh, come on! That’s exactly why we put on this play: to figure out what’s black and what’s white. And may you have days full of smiles. No nightmares!

1fd7c61dfbde00c0f9b42db755b53c72afa4ca79.en:
‘Honour’ is a brutally honest play, written with a sharp pen, humour and elegance. It delicately yet boldly explores the trials a person goes through to discover the deepest meaning of the word ‘love’. What happens when the shared values and responsibilities in a perfectly harmonious marriage suddenly begin to fade? Honour and George have been married for 32 years. Both are acclaimed authors, although poetry has taken a back seat in Onor’s life to her devotion as a wife and mother. But when the opportunity arises to revitalise one’s life, at the expense of the happiness and security of others in the family, it is as if the whole world is turned upside down. Ivaylo Hristov sets the play at a brisk pace. On the stage, designed with minimalist yet striking effect, the four wonderful actors give their all. Events flow seamlessly into one another and escalate relentlessly. Until the finale arrives – perhaps a little breathless, but deeply lyrical.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

2233d4ca10e03312890672746064ae908d00c6f0.en:
Loneliness in old age affects two-thirds of people. What do we do when the only dialogue left is the one we have with ourselves?

Dancer and choreographer Rita Gobi and puppeteer Tamás Somogyi join forces to explore the process of remembering, ageing and confronting one’s own memories. Constructed through movement without dialogue, using gestures and elements of puppetry, the performance approaches the subject with profound humanity and subtle humour.

It prompts the audience to ask themselves: when we see an elderly person, can we imagine what they were like in their youth, what dreams they had, and whether the ageing of the body also takes the soul with it?

231f80628d28379d1e081bc12387a11f3a39b71a.en: Deeply connected to nature, Norwegian director Asgeir Helgestad reveals the devastating effect of climate change on Svalbard, the fastest-warming place on Earth. Over the course of ten years, he follows the extraordinary life of Frost, a polar bear struggling to raise her cubs in a rapidly changing Arctic. This silent observation gradually becomes an intimate journey – a tale of survival and love, loss and hostility. Confronted with the consequences of human actions, Helgestad raises a fundamental question: can empathy and understanding bridge the gap between humans and animals before it is too late? Asgeir Helgestad is a renowned Norwegian director, cinematographer, screenwriter and photographer with over 30 years’ experience dedicated to documenting wildlife and the environment in the Arctic. He is one of Norway’s most award-winning wildlife photographers.

236a74ea928e1d616d136b9f519c35c281dad62c.en: ‘A Wonderful Sunday for Creve Coeur’ was written in 1975 – eight years before Tennessee Williams passed away in bizarre circumstances at a hotel in New York. As is often the case with great authors, it is as though he were writing the same play over and over again. And in this play, too, his central philosophical themes and his tender sympathy for romantics who struggle to adapt to a pragmatic existence shine ever more brightly. His Blanche from *A Streetcar Named Desire*, Laura from *The Glass Menagerie* and Hannah from *The Night of the Iguana* seem to be constantly reborn in every subsequent female character. Such is the case with Dorothea – naively devoted to a love that does not exist. Through the plot of *A Wonderful Sunday at Creve Coeur*, Williams focuses on a single morning and the encounter between four women. With comic irony and great tenderness, he skilfully explores the nightmare of loneliness, the need for human connection, and the inevitable compromises one must make to get through ‘the long race with life’. All four heroines in the play epitomise Tennessee Williams’s alchemy of character and the haunting scent of a withered rose, carried towards the hopeless and rapidly approaching twilight of romance.

24dee0483cdcef0282be5b34d0826acddd1702a7.en:
Meet Doug – the 12-year-old owner of the best trainers – and enjoy a journey back to childhood. To those lovely, endless summers when fireflies outnumber the stars in the sky, and the thrilling moments can’t be recorded in a diary because they flit past us one after the other.

The summer of 1928 – the perfect time to be a boy with new trainers! A magical moment when time seems to stand still, whilst dandelions bloom all around, apples ripen, and the meadows are mown. A summer filled with marvellous stories, memories and adventures. Carefree days of scraped knees, the scent of freshly mown grass, new soft trainers, time machines and happiness.

Douglas Spalding will discover that summer can be so much more than the past, present and future blended into one unforgettable ‘now’ that fades into the haze. Every summer, time stands still and gives us a chance to dream. This summer, however, might be different – it could be a best friend drifting away, a human time machine that can transport us back to the years of the American Civil War and its brutality. A summer of lessons learnt, dreams touched upon, and gazing at the stars to the sounds of the summer night’s heat and the songs of the cicadas and crickets in the fields…

Ana and Julio have been together for years. However, the passage of time and the daily routine have driven them apart, seemingly irrevocably. They no longer look at one another or touch each other, and arguments between them have become the norm.

Until they move into a new flat… A flat where screams and moans can constantly be heard from the floor above. Perhaps out of jealousy, perhaps out of envy and a longing for a more exciting life, but these sounds become the subject of constant arguments between Ana and Julio.

Without telling her husband, Ana invites the neighbours from upstairs round so they can get to know each other and become friends. Julio insists they should complain about the noise, but Ana doesn’t want to bother them.

The evening turns into a comical clash between the sexual liberality of the neighbours upstairs and Julio and Ana’s ‘conventional’ way of socialising and living. The couple face a serious test, as their upstairs neighbours turn their world upside down.

An emotional storm of mutual accusations erupts, bringing hidden grievances and repressed desires to the surface. Tonight, the neighbours will become both the instigators and the victims of an emotional tsunami, triggered by an unusually bold and surprising proposal.

How to carry on after such an ‘intense’ evening – that is the question facing Ana and Julio!

2bc5c0dd36472f98af0106695a0616de983f9683.en:
‘A Streetcar Named Desire’ is one of Tennessee Williams’ most remarkable plays, which has left a truly significant mark on the history of world literature and theatre.

The plot follows the story of Blanche DuBois (Veselina Konakchiska), who decides to escape her personal problems by going to stay with her younger sister Stella (Nia Krasteva) and her husband Stanley Kowalski (Vladimir Karamazov) in New Orleans.

Blanche’s mind and heart are in turmoil and, despite her attempt to escape, her past catches up with her. Stanley’s boorish and rude behaviour only serves to make her days even harder to bear.

The conflict between the two is the thread in the play that can be interpreted in various ways and justified by various means. Every stage production of *A Streetcar Named Desire* arouses excitement and curiosity in the audience, who are eager to see how these characters, brimming with such intense emotions, problems and needs, come to life on stage.

The story that Tennessee Williams created continues to captivate readers and audiences years after its creation, precisely because it tackles themes that will always be relevant and significant, placing a strong emphasis on human vulnerability and those inner struggles that can lead to utter ruin.

2c157861e50f38ae88cfac1a6669ea775603d788.en:
Edward Albee’s play *Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?* continues to capture the public’s interest almost 60 years after its first performance. What is more, these days, discussing the intimate issues at the heart of the play is becoming increasingly important, because personal space seems to have been abandoned in modern life. Caught up in the web of the globalised world, people lose their sensitivity to close, direct contact. And this insensitivity breeds violence.

With exceptional skill, blending the comic with the tragic, the author makes us witnesses to a night-time scene in which two couples, in the words of the characters themselves, ‘peel off the labels’ and ‘get right to the bone’ in their relationships.

The scene is captivating and leads to a classic catharsis – a cleansing of repressed emotions through regret and fear, through tears and laughter.

2c9b5d4546ff0148b82c45c60d563cb67f326b10.en:
If you associate power primarily with money, influence, corruption, abuse and illegality, listen to this: “Power comes slowly. First it seeps in through the pores, into the posture, into the chest, into the corner of the mouth, until it takes over the whole body.”

These words are part of the latest performance by Iva Sveshtarova and Vili Prager, which leads us to reflect on power through the body – a body in whose memory it pulsates, not as an idea, but as a muscle, a habit, a breath. The two choreographers transform the body from an instrument of violence into a territory of vulnerability, whilst reshaping power into new, seemingly harmless forms. It becomes theatre – grandiose, merciless, absurd. In *Bodies of Power*, the bodies are props, the chorus is the people, and the stage is life itself.

Watching the performance, you will inevitably ask yourself: haven’t I seen this before? Yes, you most likely have – in archive photographs, interviews and reports from institutions, in courtrooms and court rulings, in draft legislation and regulations.

The performance is not funny, despite the amusing moments it contains. It remains unclear what exactly it is making fun of – the body or power, politics or society. The only thing that is clear is that it all begins with an execution.

2cca3f793540eff8e7365ec9c8db3ad5fa8207c2.en:
Linda – a young woman who still lives with her parents in a provincial Danish country house – unexpectedly takes her own life. Her twin brother, as well as her younger brother and sister, who have long since moved out on their own, are baffled as to why she took her own life. The whole family is devastated.

The funeral passes, the pain gradually begins to subside, and their father’s anniversary looms on the horizon. The whole family gathers at the family estate to mark the occasion.

The celebrations get off to a promising start, and family harmony is on the verge of being restored after the deep wounds inflicted by the untimely loss. All the family members – lovers of sharp humour, mutual sarcastic jibes and cheeky jokes – – gradually let their guard down and get swept up in the festive spirit, until the twin brother of Linda, who took her own life, decides to give a speech that turns everything on its head.

A man may well be living the good life, but sooner or later the time comes when he has to get married. Unless, of course, his beloved runs off before they reach the altar…

Is this the greatest misfortune or the greatest stroke of luck? Nobody knows.

Instead of hearing the long-awaited ‘I do!’ and dancing at a lavish wedding, you suddenly find yourself in a world of bloody battles, missing front teeth, unexpected friendships and painfully funny truths about love, marriage and the male ego.

2e976c1040b76950d0d8f6fc098313b724a57b30.en:
It might not sound realistic, but that’s only because you’ve never been stuck in… THE LIFT.

This is the story of two strangers forced to spend the night together in a broken-down lift, stuck between floors. She has to get home at all costs. He’s running late. And time is running out. Is it chance or a twist of fate that brings them together?

Four walls and two people create a new reality, demanding answers they are not ready to give.

What is the price of freedom? Are we afraid of the truth? Can we break free from the prejudices and rules that define us?

A dead-end situation becomes the only way out for two people who want to escape but cannot. How long can this illusion last? Will we hide from reality, or will the lift doors open and time continue its course?

‘The Lift’ is a play that offers no easy answers.

It confronts the characters – and the audience – with a choice: the security of the familiar or the risk of the unknown? Sometimes the way out lies not in the outside world, but in what changes within us.

The question that remains is not whether we will get out, but what we will be like when we do.

2f04f9e02e1099e3c8bd89bbb226b10774353a25.en:
In *The Cry of an Angel*, a small man desperately raises big questions. Desperately, because he has been unable to answer them, unable to cope with life, and even says that he has not really lived it. That is why, of his own free will, he renounces his own will.

The action takes place in Bulgaria, and the reasons for his misfortunes are as much personal as they are, more broadly, Bulgarian. The little man discusses them as such. And, as is traditional in our part of the world, it doesn’t seem as though there’s any way things can get better.

It is possible that viewers may find it difficult to identify with the protagonist because, as we have said, we are talking about a ‘little man’, and there aren’t many ‘little men’ left – we all think we’re a big deal. Most likely, a quick connection can be made with the reproaches he sometimes makes. Reproaching is contagious.

But the true value of this text, at least according to the production team, does not stem from the pathos of the bleak observations shared by the great men, but shines through in the acknowledged helplessness of the little man, living not here or there, but on Earth.

For when you realise how small you are beneath the boundless starry sky, then a greater meaning may be discovered, distinct from the appearances that drive you to engage in unnecessary struggles, regardless of the means. Then the devastating greed and cruelty, over which the angel weeps, may vanish.

To be honest with the audience, we deliberately refrain from the game of role-play and simply tell the story of the desperate little man whom we can scarcely reach. Let this theatrical device be seen as a gesture of humility.

Lower the curtain! I beg your pardon, I forgot that only a select few can write plays and have the right to perform on stage. I have broken the monopoly!

These are the words of the suicidal Konstantin Treplev, spoken after his performance in the first act of the play *The Seagull*. Just as the character says ‘Lower the curtain!’, we raise it…

The performance is a four-act investigation, with a prologue and an epilogue, about our rejection of a dead, marginal presence within the theatre community. We relive the story of the son from Chekhov’s drama, of the artist – as our representative, as a representative of the searching artists of the independent theatre scene.

We are confronted with the fact that not all lives are of equal value; not all lives are equally worthy of mourning. We are off stage.

33903dd9f621ca7294e908bbf9405a28bf3488c1.en:
“Cries from the Underground” is a play based on Dostoevsky’s “Notes from the Underground”.

Nietzsche wrote that in these notes, the truth is not presented as philosophical reasoning, but cries out in pain, because only in this way can the truth manifest itself. That is why we are turning the text into a play – so that it may happen, be experienced, rather than simply be read.

‘The Underground Man’ probes his own wound, reaches the point of complete self-exposure, and acknowledges his utter disagreement with the established world and its laws, whilst not sparing his own guilt and powerlessness. There is no salvation, unless this candid confession is salvation itself.

In the preface to *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, Nietzsche speaks of ‘the last man’. He seeks comfort, not meaning; he avoids suffering and risk; for him there is no God, no truth, no purpose other than cynical comfort; he lives a long but shallow life. It is as though Nietzsche were describing modern man.

We propose an encounter between this modern man and the underground figure, and we believe the effect will be, to say the least, thrilling.

33f30800d4916bd520013f4c8bef204222469b64.en: ‘The Comedy of Errors’ draws us into a labyrinth of unknowns, into a whirlwind of confusing situations bordering on dreams. Were it not for the exceptional humour woven into Shakespeare’s language, this story would resemble more of a schizophrenic nightmare – lost identities, split personalities, role reversals, separated families, partners swapped… In a world populated by ‘liars and charlatans’, two twin brothers who have never met constantly miss each other, wandering through the ‘sea of people’ that constantly engulfs them. The closer they are to one another, the further apart they drift, and each, slowly but surely, changes himself and takes on the other’s role. They take on a new – seemingly uncharacteristic – image, but one which, deep down, feels familiar. What happens to a person who has lost their roots, their very essence? How can we restore our lost inner harmony? How can we bring order to the chaos? And can we, in fact, be ourselves without knowing ourselves fully?

The play *Lisbon* by the writer and playwright Zachary Karabashliev is being performed for the first time for a Bulgarian audience, in its full version, at the ‘Nikolay Binev’ Youth Theatre.

This also marks Yana Titova’s grand return to the Youth Theatre, though this time in the role of director.

The play “Lisbon” weaves together themes of freedom, identity and the impossibility of escaping our own prisons.

A group of people have been abducted and locked away in an unknown, undefined place. Whilst they wait to be told the amount of their ransom, they are condemned to be together and – whether they like it or not – to interact with one another. But how long will they spend there – hours? Days? Years? And where is this unknown place?

355a159d4c943c1203e0e91e1bfc4b9f74db40d2.en: There is a legend which tells that once, in ancient times, the gods created man and woman as a single being. These androgynous beings lived in harmony, contentment and ecstasy, but the gods grew bored and, for amusement, separated the men from the women and scattered them across the whole earth. Seized by panic, everyone rushed to seek out their other halves to restore wholeness, harmony and ecstasy. This is how it is today, and this is how it has been throughout the centuries. This frantic quest has fuelled thousands of literary works. There are many dramas and tragedies, but there are also many comic situations arising from this confusion and our desire to overcome it. Jean-Baptiste Molière, the master of 17th-century French comedy and of all time, offers us two enchanting plays – gems that remain so in world drama to this day. ‘Georges Dandin, or The Cuckold’ and ‘Sganarelle, the Cuckold Without Horns’, have been combined into a single production entitled ‘The Cuckolds’, because in both plays the main plot revolves once again around that eternal quest to find one’s lost other half.

A tragic tale of the complex journey – fraught with dramatic obstacles – of a former prisoner who served time for two murders. A confession about the protagonist’s catharsis and spiritual enlightenment, about the light and strength that love and faith bestow upon him.

‘THE BELL’ is a play that shakes the audience emotionally and uplifts them spiritually, drawing them out of the comfort of being mere observers and immersing them in intense passions through striking depictions of the harsh realities of life. The action on stage grips us with the powerful energy of Deyan Donkov’s total acting transformation.

364976203f23ceac1111f5621f3b99792c441cb8.en:
The latest solo piece by international choreographer Zornitsa Stoyanova, *Honesty and Other Fiends*, combines contemporary dance, stand-up comedy, poetry and visual effects. Having premiered in the US in 2024, with performances in the Netherlands, the show is now also in Bulgaria. Through humour and irony, *Honesty and Other Fiends* reveals the horror of humanity’s obsession with grandeur. The performance raises the question of honesty as a personal and social value in the age of ‘alternative facts’, transforming the thinking body into an act of resistance.

Stoyanova blends movement, personal stories and absurdism in a raw and entertaining solo that confronts the death of ‘Truth’ and reveals what remains. She dances and plays games with the audience, peeling back layers of her communist identity in a meditation on truth, power and the female body. This is a bold, new political solo, blending contemporary dance and stand-up comedy. The performance is in English.

In a small university town, the artist Evelyn has won a commission to create a sculptural installation. At the Museum of Art, she meets Adam, a scruffy man in his thirties who juggles his work commitments as a security guard at the museum, a sales assistant at the university bookshop and his role as co-author of a book he is writing with his best friend, Philip. Adam’s relationship with Evelyn leads not only to his physical transformation, but also to a series of changes in his way of life. Adam’s transformation into a popular and attractive man does not go unnoticed by his closest friends, leading to unexpected changes in both his personal and social life. In his new self, the young man finds himself entangled in the subtle, almost invisible web of the dangerous transformation to which all forms of art lead.

398388964fbda7d451589cc221508857e7303d9d.en:
‘Ah, those ghosts!’ is one of Eduardo De Filippo’s most iconic and beloved comedies, in which the line between reality and illusion is as thin as smoke. The story takes us to a huge, empty Neapolitan palace, rumoured to be haunted by ghosts. Pasquale is a man with a noble heart, but plagued by poverty. He moves in as a tenant, hoping to turn it into a guesthouse. When inexplicable things begin to happen and ‘gifts’ from the afterlife start appearing in the house, Pasquale chooses to believe in miracles rather than the bitter truth. Because sometimes it is easier to believe in a ghost than to face the truth head-on.

A play about the human need to delude ourselves in order to survive. With plenty of smiles and the eternal question: which are the real ghosts – those that roam the rooms, or those we hide within our own souls?

3b2149543c2b9e5d46a4738e1c1be50382c4698f.en: At the Comédie-Française, preparations are in full swing for a production of *Macbeth*, Shakespeare’s famous tragedy. But just three hours before Nina’s directorial debut, complete chaos ensues – first the technical equipment fails, then the weaknesses and selfish outbursts of the actors in the troupe threaten to ruin the premiere. As the tension backstage mounts, Nina begins to see visions of Molière himself, who reproaches her for staging Shakespeare rather than one of his own plays. Caught between hallucination and reality, between attempts to calm the actors and her helpless baby, Nina resolves to keep the show going at any cost. Because the golden rule of the ‘Comédie-Française’ is never to cancel a performance. But does dedication always pay off? And is it possible for a play like *Macbeth*, whose central themes are betrayal and the corruption of power, to be interpreted as a comedy?

3d88f95ef631d1514efbc143ca29960bb068bda8.en: The story begins in Trigrad – the heart of the Rhodopes, where ancient legends, music and the mountains intertwine. It is here that the gaida reveals itself not merely as a musical instrument, but as a spiritual bridge between people, cultures and generations. The main character, Mitko, lost his younger brother, Yuli, several years earlier. In the final months of his life, the only thing that managed to lift Yuli from the burden of his illness was his desire to learn to play the gaida. After his death, Mitko follows in his footsteps – he takes up the bagpipes and embarks on a personal journey in memory of his brother, seeking meaning, solace and a bond that cannot be broken. The film follows this extraordinary journey, which connects Bulgaria and California through the power of music and brotherly love. From the Rhodopes, the story takes us to Los Angeles, where Mitko meets three extraordinary individuals – the bagpiper Eric Riegler, whose performances feature in the film *Braveheart*, the Bulgarian bagpiper Petro Dushkov; and the technological visionary and collector of musical instruments from around the world, Jaron Lanier. Each of these encounters reveals different possibilities of the gaida as a musical instrument and its extraordinary impact on people who, on the surface, inhabit completely different worlds. The journey concludes with a return to Bulgaria, to the village of Gela, where we meet the masters of the bagpipe who keep this centuries-old art alive. Thus, the film becomes a story of memory, hope and the power of music to connect people across time and distance.

3d94857e01d98f802512044ec2ddccc18d2a2ac5.en:
‘No Problem’ is a comedy about conversation as a game, about words as a strategy, and about those little deviations from the truth that we make to keep the conversation going a little longer. Two strangers meet again and again – each time with a slight change, a new version of themselves, a different answer to the same questions.

The scenes repeat themselves, the lines are rearranged, and reality turns out to be flexible – depending on who we are at that moment and what we’re prepared to say to be liked. Amidst the awkward flirting, the little white lies, the sincere confessions and the sudden twists, the play traces how conversation becomes a battleground, and ‘no problem’ – a universal excuse.

With humour and sharp observations, ‘No Problem’ raises questions about loneliness, intimacy and the need to adapt to others without losing ourselves. A comedy about the modern city dweller, about encounters that could have unfolded in a thousand different ways, and about that one moment when everything seems possible.

How much does it take for a person to lose their balance? Sometimes, just a silly joke.

A present, a few people, and a situation that could have been over in a matter of minutes, had everyone not been so determined to complicate it.

‘The Gift’ is a comedy about our astonishing talent for turning minor annoyances into monumental disasters. It’s about the decisions we make in an attempt to sort things out, when in fact we’re only making the situation more hopeless.

Because sometimes the biggest problem is that we just can’t leave things alone.

A practical workshop with Rita Gobi from Hungary for professional actors.

Can movement transform dramaturgy, reshape the text and reveal new possibilities for theatrical expression? What happens to a theatrical genre when the body becomes the primary vehicle for meaning?

Through work with movement, gesture, rhythm, space and physical presence, participants will explore how the body can create its own dramaturgy and expand the boundaries of the genre and theatrical expression.

The workshop invites actors to discover new possibilities on stage by exploring the body as a source of action, image and meaning.

3fea55c8c036e0dc43f79b508d7a4f2d1c0467bd.en: The plot of the play takes us back to the 17th century. The story begins in 1640 and ends in 1655 with the death of Cyrano (Kamen Donev). He is a universally recognised poetic talent, a cadet in the French army, whom everyone admires for his keen sense of justice, his incorruptibility, his love of the theatre and his fiery temper. Few dare to speak out against him, for he is the finest fencer in Paris and readily engages in duels, even when outnumbered. But to his cousin Roxana (Louizabel Nikolova), with whom he is hopelessly in love, he is a kind, amusing and warm-hearted friend. The fearless cadet does not dare to reveal his feelings. The reason for this is his large nose. His outward ugliness contrasts with the tender impulses of his poetic soul. One day, Roxane confides in Cyrano that she has fallen in love and, in an ironic twist of fate, her chosen one – Christian de Neuville (Yasen Atanasov) – is a handsome young soldier serving in his own regiment. Cyrano’s chivalry compels him to grant her request and take the young man under his wing. Christian confides in him his lack of confidence in communicating with Roxane, who is far more intelligent than he is. Cyrano then strikes a strange bargain, offering to ‘lend him his eloquence’ and begins writing letters to his cousin, which Christian signs. It is precisely these letters that capture Roxane’s imagination, but she continues to believe that Christian is the man with whom she is corresponding. However, the wealthy and influential Count de Guiche (Georgi Kirkalanov)—commander of the regiment in which Cyrano and Christian serve—is also in love with her. To save her from the Count’s advances, Cyrano himself arranges her hasty marriage to Christian, but the young man dies very soon on the battlefield, and with him goes Cyrano’s secret. Roxane enters a convent. Cyrano visits her, but never reveals the truth about her great love. ‘Unbowed by meanness, lies, envy, compromise or money’, Cyrano meets his death at the hands of the enemy with his head held high. It is only at this sublime and, at the same time, tragic moment that the woman he adored realises who the tender poet is, the one who had captured her heart forever. Cyrano – a hero of romantic fervour who cares nothing for wealth and, without bowing to authority, follows his own path, sacrificing his personal happiness in the name of a higher ideal.

40efd258986462422906638b7aa3e1f8f82f18ce.en:
Theophilus is a successful, celebrity author, though his fame has faded considerably of late. Longing to move away from his image as the author of saccharine romantic novels, he writes a short poetic tale about a little sea snail that has lost its shell and is searching for the meaning of life.

To his own surprise, Theophilus rediscovers his inspiration in the process, but has no idea what effect this story will have on those close to him. As if looking in a mirror, they begin to recognise themselves in the characters – sea urchins, prawns, mermaids and other sea creatures – and discover hidden messages in the metaphors.

That evening, everyone gathers to settle their scores. And it turns into a veritable cataclysm. One after another, the family members pour out everything that’s weighing on them, lay bare their fears and speak their minds, triggering a torrent of comical and surreal misunderstandings and miscommunications.

Leonor Confino’s ‘Mirror, Mirror’ is a witty contemporary comedy about 21st-century humanity, living in an age of ever-increasing alienation, raising the fundamental question of whether we, as human beings, are capable of seeing the world as it is, or whether we see it solely through the reflection of who we ourselves are.

40efd686a4c31db7df6cd037a07c24f208bebc64.en:
The Bulgarian people are surrounded on all sides by Vazov. He has given a name to everything in the Bulgarian world. That is why, from age to age, our mountains will remain just as high and blue, our departed will pass into another realm, our beloved homeland will remain beautiful, its songs will always be sung, the language of our forefathers will be sacred, and our mothers will be our mothers twice over. His words are our anchor in a world intoxicated by the abolition of God, homeland and kin; a world full of fickle souls, without faith in our historical existence. Through Vazov’s words we understand ourselves: as we do not know ourselves, as we find it hard to accept ourselves, as we do not believe ourselves to be. That is why the question ‘Where is Bulgaria?’ is not a question of geography, but of existence.

Alexander Sekulov

The particular challenge in working on this production is its scale. The theatre rarely tackles military conflicts, national catastrophes and ethnic tragedies due to the specific nature of its artistic means. Even less so when it comes to an epic narrative in which not only individual people, but entire social and cultural strata of the nation exist independently, move and intertwine. And this narrative is set against a specific historical moment, about which, even a hundred years on, the debates continue. But above all stood our inner duty to present Ivan Vazov as an eternally living figure, to look at ourselves through his eyes, and once again to fall silent before his power to chart our destiny as a people.

4311d4778648ef5dc8da8c9b8646920e4fe4d37c.en:
What is right, and in whose eyes? Can we so easily categorise things as ‘good’ or ‘bad’? Do we have the right to enter someone else’s world and pass judgement? Should anyone have to apologise for having their own understanding, for having different ideas about life…? For loving in their own way, which doesn’t obey any rules… Do we have the right to pry into the soul of someone we don’t understand?!

Who are we to judge?!

This is a play about love, about complete devotion and union. About sacrifice and self-sacrifice. About the mother. About family. About values. About complete self-denial in the name of what is most precious and beloved, about duty to what you believe in. About physical death, which brings living death to the living lover. And about physical death as a deliverance from living death. A play about the inner conflicts between conscience, the law and the heart. About the disconnect… About the mystery that is me, you, each of us for ourselves and each of us for others…

44d8e204027da75326326f8910ccb1a247f8f3fc.en:
Evolution has done a remarkable job with our social brain. It just failed to leave a user manual. Ever since, we have been trying to understand how neurons give rise to morality, reason and society. Sometimes this endeavour grows into two books.

How has evolution made sociality an integral part of human nature? What makes a judgement rational, given that emotions are also involved? Where does morality come from? And when an intellectual dilemma presents us with a choice, who actually decides? Is it us, or the homunculus we have so conveniently installed behind the control panel in our heads?

The occasion for this conversation is the launch of the two volumes of *Neurosociology*:

‘Neurosociology: From Neuron to Society’ and ‘Neurosociology: Ratio moralis’, published by St Clement of Ohrid University Press.

At the heart of these books lies an attempt to rebuild a long-lost bridge between neuroscience and sociology. To seek out the biological and evolutionary roots of human sociality, morality, emotions and rationality. Not to reduce society to neurons, but because the social world can hardly be understood if we ignore the brain that makes it possible.

The evening is intended to be a free-flowing intellectual conversation, rather than an exercise in formal speeches. I look forward to hearing different perspectives, questions and arguments from the audience that might challenge some of our preconceived notions. In science, this is usually helpful, though not always pleasant.

4769be8d7ae26222e68a983a3eb0362fcd83ad85.en: Fifteen stab wounds in 27 seconds. This is what Salman Rushdie went through before opening his only functioning eye and looking at the camera. Together with his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths, the writer decided to document his slow return to life a few days after the brutal attack in New York. Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney unfolds a painful and deeply insightful story that traces Salman Rushdie’s rehabilitation and pays tribute to his indomitable spirit, humour and optimism. The story begins following the publication of *The Satanic Verses*, when a religious edict, a ‘fatwa’, was issued against Rushdie by the Iranian Ayatollah Khomeini. From that moment on, the writer lived under constant threat for decades, fighting for the right to free public expression. The culmination of the persecution is captured in a harrowing recording of the assassination attempt… Rushdie will return to the scene of the crime to bring this dark chapter of his life to a close, but is that even possible? A powerfully resonant documentary narrative that explores the themes of religion and art as an explosive combination. Salman Rushdie, a brilliant writer and intellectual with a cosmopolitan spirit, reflects on violence, forgiveness and the right to free speech – themes that are more relevant than ever.

47837d59e5b2585b7b1019f8b78b6e18d111e0eb.en: Nora, Thomas and their daughter Ida live peacefully on a secluded farm. Their only neighbour is the Italian artist Cristina (Monica Bellucci). Whilst everyone is preparing for a surprise party to celebrate Nora’s birthday, three suspicious men begin loitering around the house. Before long, they take it upon themselves to join the celebrations. Tranquillity gives way to anxiety and tension. The film is an adaptation of the noir novel of the same name by Laurent Mouvignier – a skilfully layered socio-psychological narrative structured as a crime thriller. The author puts forward the idea that dangers and anxieties do not strike suddenly, but slowly seep into everyday life. As the characters’ pasts come to light, it turns out that almost every one of them bears the burden of some form of remorse, fear, past humiliation or unresolved trauma. Laurent Mouvignier is one of the most highly regarded contemporary authors in France and has recently cemented his status as a brilliant novelist by winning the prestigious Goncourt Prize for his monumental novel *The Empty House*. The film is not recommended for children under 16.

47f54e957a12bedcba4f323d3525ce6285e731eb.en:
An airport is a place where nobody pays any attention to those around them. Everyone is focused on a different goal, carrying their own story, their own pain, hope or dream, and has no time to look around. Suitcases pass each other by, flights are delayed, and anonymity is comforting, almost a lifeline.

But what would happen if, for a moment, time stood still? If the noise died down and people realised they weren’t alone? If, for a brief moment, they managed to see the light that others carry, even complete strangers?

‘Airport’ is the place where this happens. A place of meetings and partings, of missed chances and second chances. The production intertwines the fates of several, at first glance, random travellers, whose lives intersect in a timeless space between ‘before’ and ‘after’. In this suspended moment, they find the courage to say the unsaid, to forgive, to say goodbye or, even if only briefly, to choose a new direction.

‘Airport’ is a story about human connection – the kind that arises unexpectedly, burns brightly and changes everything. Because sometimes all it takes is a single glance, a single word or a single encounter to realise that you are not always travelling alone.

47fd534f0cfea83f5ea7d0de2fc5f5154d9205ab.en: In the 1970s, ten-year-old Ida lived in a remote village in the Slovenian countryside with her parents and her beloved grandmother, who was her greatest source of support. One day, her grandmother fainted whilst watering the flowers at the local cemetery. Ida panics, but suddenly hears a mysterious, angelic song. Her grandmother miraculously recovers, and the girl is amazed by the power of the song. Convinced that singing could save her grandmother’s life, Ida decides to join the school choir, even though she cannot sing. After the audition, she is rejected, but a shy girl named Terezka will try to help her. Through the lens of childhood loneliness, I wanted to explore the space between the lightness of everyday life and the quiet presence of inevitable loss. Faced with this feeling, children seek refuge in their imagination, in play, in solitude or in moments shared with friends, and find security wherever they can. The film unfolds precisely in these fleeting moments, in which innocence and vulnerability coexist. Esther Ivačić

4803808eb8084008e0be0352faf133a0b79fe4bd.en: “The Magical Night Before Christmas” is a show about the power of faith, family and the Christmas spirit. It’s about how we mustn’t give up, despite the doubts we sometimes feel. It’s about the relationships between parents and children, and how important the warmth of home is – something we so often feel at Christmas with our families. A story that follows the journey of little Tony, for whom Christmas is the most special of all holidays, but on this ‘magical night’ he finds himself in danger. 486294403d756a181f13c18eef5023b30c100f8c.en:
The production is based on challenges that are fundamental to us, which we discovered in three books: *Manifesto of New Realism* by Maurizio Ferraris, *The Theatre and Its Double* by Antonin Artaud, and *Realism* by Kerstin Strömel. We didn’t even manage to finish reading some of them.

At a time when all contemporary discussions revolve around politics and identity, the phenomenon of post-truth and the rise of populism, our team distances itself from these pervasive trends. At a time when everything is changing at breakneck speed, the team is preoccupied with its own centrifugal forces and their external manifestations.

The performance aims to inspire or dismantle the intentions and rough edges between the individual segments: choreography, dance, dramaturgy, direction, musical scores, presence, costumes, props, light, shadows, songs, manifestos and all manner of components and techniques that our team employs, because they require quotations, references and models. We produce in order to create a world that can easily be destroyed. Is that what we want?
