Danceperimental – the performance that’s never the same twice! (and that’s precisely why you can watch it as many times as you like!)

Danceperimental (the latest format from the Muzotants Dance Company) is an interactive dance performance with live music that involves the audience in the creative process. The boundary between artists and audience is broken down by an old telephone, which challenges the audience to take part in creating the performance with their personal stories, whilst each audience member decides for themselves whether to join in or not. The dance and music are entirely improvised, emerging in the moment, in and from the presence of the audience, and inspired by what they share.

Since 2022, Danceperimental has been gaining increasing popularity. It has been performed over 20 times on various stages in the capital and beyond. In 2024, it was invited to the ‘Dance Routes’ Contemporary Dance Festival in Varna, and in 2025 it became part of the programme at the RCSI ‘Toplocentral’ with regular performances, having been selected through an open call for completed productions.

Over the years, the creative team has comprised seven dancers and two musicians, and the format continues to evolve and develop.

How far can a person go when no one has heard their cry?

This is a play about everything that happens to a person when, for a long time, they have nowhere to turn with their pain.

About the point of no return.

About violence, which never comes without consequences.

‘RAGE’ introduces us to a group of teenagers who stand before us with their darkest thoughts. With everything they have been through, with the trauma they carry, with the words that remain deep within them. They are victims of circumstance, of differences, of a lack of understanding. Confused, hurt and alone in their attempts to find a way to cope with the world and with themselves.

Stephen King published his novel *Rage* in 1977. Since then, much has changed, but much has remained the same. They say we live in troubled times. I wonder how many times since then people have said the same thing, and how many more times they will continue to do so.

The story of Charlie Decker from Stephen King’s novel is told through an encounter between the protagonist and his creator – the writer. They look back and reveal a story that gradually becomes a mirror of the world in which we live.

‘RAGE’ depicts a reality in which it is becoming increasingly difficult for us to understand one another, whilst young people are left alone amidst their own fears and confusion. They seek freedom, justice and connection. They seek someone who will listen to them.

And sometimes, when they find no answer, anger begins to speak for them.

4ceeebb517ae4af92c781ffb4ce2ac7730e12b5e.en:
What happens when three women set off on a two-day hike in the mountains, somewhat ‘against their will’? Naturally, they open up to each other – though not about everything – then, for no apparent reason, they have a row and, unsurprisingly, make up; they get ‘a bit’ tipsy; they pretend to hate each other, but deep down they love each other very much. Yes, at first glance it’s complete chaos of emotions, but we women call it friendship. And however much men may excite us, there’s something they can’t give us, and that’s precisely this scattered jumble of emotions in which we manage not to lose ourselves.

Two days during which three women make important decisions and overcome obstacles that lead to absurd and touching situations between them. Will they tell each other the truth? Will they find the strength to forgive one another? Will they survive in this hostile environment?

Step by step, we’ll walk with them towards the summit, where they must say their final farewell to their late friend.

And yet: What happens on the mountain stays on the mountain!

Lisa Shopova

The plot of the play ‘STEP BY STEP’ weaves together a whole host of touching and funny situations. Step by step, the play traces the challenges facing the friendship of three women.

Their encounter with nature and the unexpected difficulties they face turn into comical encounters with the struggles of the modern woman in our fast-paced world, who has no time either to look within herself and fully reveal her feelings, nor to understand those close to her.

How many secrets and unspoken grievances might lie hidden behind this professed closeness?

4d2781709002a8eed09e55cfa66c43bc7c91da95.en:
All the lofty dreams of 20th-century theatre – from the yearning to ‘shatter illusions’ to Peter Brook’s ‘total theatre’ and Heiner Müller’s ‘playing with realities as a subversive act’ – are embodied and realised in the dramaturgy of Samuel Beckett. His poetic ‘theatrical machines’ – at once human beings and fallen angels, trapped in their existential snares – buried in the ground; living in rubbish bins or cylinders – are a replica of the martyrs from Dante’s ‘Inferno’. Except that they are punished without having sinned. Punished to live.

Beckett’s theatre might be called a cruel theatre, a theatre of the inevitable. A theatre for the lost man, ‘cast aside’ into existence, doomed to the ‘eternal today’.

Man, taken in his pure identity with his unanswered questions, his agitated consciousness, powerless to untangle the insoluble knots between a life that is slipping away and all-pervading death. Things and nothingness.

The mouth as if mad, the tongue as a response to the absurdity of human existence, shattered by pauses through which one glimpses – what?!

Pain as a modus vivendi; as salvation from the void. The other as the sole support.

Amongst the gallery of Beckett’s clowns – the two ‘lucky ones’, Winnie and Willie, occupy a special place.

Like the universal soul from Chekhov’s *The Seagull*, Winnie does not know ‘who she is or what awaits her’, but she has taken in ‘the whole of life, the whole of life, the whole of life’ and bears its heavy blessing as a miracle for which she is responsible. Like an overflowing precious cup from which not a single drop must be wasted. There is no whingeing, no grumbling.

512928b5e7168ed4d3727f5866b88810435fac64.en:
‘KARAKONJUL’ is a tragicomic reflection on an extraordinary fate: Ramadan Dervishov, the character made famous by Nikolay Haytov’s short story ‘Dervish’s Seed’, shares his life story with the bear he has tamed, but above all with the audience: married at the tender age of 14, he loses his beloved and his love, consumed by grief and a passion for revenge – yet, through many inner struggles and hesitations, he finds his way back to himself. He carves it out with difficulty – for he is a wild and unruly man, hewn like a mountain rock. He argues with Mayor Chatalbashev, he recalls the first moments of his marriage, which is in fact a child’s game; he longs to be by his beloved wife’s side, and this sometimes humbles him, whilst at other times it makes him great in his devotion to her. He is brimming with natural strength, with naive yet wise discoveries, with stories of events so funny they bring tears to the eyes – stories that broaden our understanding of the power and meaning of the human being and their frenzied struggles with and for life.

Shut away in his mountain hut and in his unfulfilled heartache, Ramadan Dervishov shares himself and his primal experience as if with the whole world – with people near and far, chance acquaintances and close friends, neighbours and fellow villagers, with nature and domestic animals – and in doing so, he enriches and fills human existence with excitement and events, with naivety and wisdom, with pain and laughter.

It is no coincidence that KARAKONJUL is the nickname given to someone plagued by insomnia. The encounter with the protagonist Ramadan is a truly sleepless and fascinating one...

5139dbece01ca4b94e4d275ec1b73ef380e3e526.en:
The Cannes Film Festival! The most glamorous of all possible occasions for celebration. In the late afternoon, just a few hours before the triumphant premiere of her latest film, the lifeless body of the last true diva of the international film scene was discovered on the terrace of a luxury hotel – Grace Jerves.

The cast of suspected murderers is impressively colourful and even amusing: an extravagant actor, a jealous impresario, a flamboyant blonde and a novice thief. Each of them has their own version of what happened, and every one of them is ready to instantly rewrite the chronology of events, just to get their hands on the murdered star’s diamonds. Only the hotel manager – Monsieur Boniface, an unproven descendant of Hercule Poirot, is able to uncover the truth amidst the thickening fog of delusions, clumsy lies and lustful thoughts.

The lively French Riviera has never before

witnessed such an unpredictable series of irreversible events!

Never has Hollywood offered such a catalogue of criminal

conspiracies! Is it possible that real life can be so

unrestrained, or is it simply that when you throw a few

celebrities together, things are bound to spiral out of control?

Comedy or crime thriller – the choice is yours! Or why not both?

530fe1978f17d4c33ef13be36951a34c8cf5fc71.en:
‘SHE’ is a film shot using an observational approach over a period of four years – a documentary diary of three women – Olya, Olena and Nina, of different ages and ethnic backgrounds, whose husbands serve in the 88th Marine Battalion of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. After 24 February, the war and Bolhrad brought them together. There, they built a new community based on mutual support, female solidarity and inner strength.

This is a story about the long wait for Victory, about the men on the front line, about the daily news and about life spent in constant anticipation, during which each of the heroines undergoes a transformation. The naïve belief in a swift Victory gives way to the endless absence of a loved one, to the vast distances, to antidepressants and to telephone calls.

This is a story about life continuing in the shelters, in voluntary work, in the constant anticipation of the message: ‘He’s alive’. This is a story about love that is forced to mature alongside the war and which helps them, despite everything, to stay together.

The film depicts all the consequences of war – everything as it is in our present: faith gives way to despair, optimism to hopelessness, laughter to tears. The birth of a new life and the burial of a life cut short go hand in hand.

53f5c42b16082c92f8551f527d98f7e9fbdbc817.en:
The harrowing story of Dr Ralph Greenson’s final psychoanalytic session with the unforgettable actress and American icon, Marilyn Monroe. What happened after their meeting at her home on 5 August 1962, that led to Marilyn being found dead just hours later? What led to this tragic outcome?

The play by Dr Vivian Pramataroff-Hamburger and Prof. Andreas Hamburger, based on authentic documents and events, reveals the true, dramatic essence of the great star Marilyn, hidden behind the façade of the seductive blonde desired by millions of Americans. Childhood traumas, failed marriages, the gruelling grind of film sets, alcohol and barbiturates, her entanglement in the web of high politics and her dangerous connections with the Kennedy brothers bring Marilyn together with the renowned scientist and psychoanalyst Dr Ralph Greenson, who also has his own hidden family drama, yet he devotedly tries to help the young woman, even crossing the acceptable boundaries in their relationship.

A production that looks beyond the glittering façade of the legend and delves into the very essence of the unhappy woman, Marilyn.

554aa024425161626faa9664f883e77604cd3411.en:
This is a story about heroic people who risk their lives to bring light to the Ukrainian people – just like Prometheus. This is a story about the last operational power station in eastern Ukraine, situated in the free part of the Donetsk region. The power station is situated 10 km from the front line and, as a result, is subjected to constant and intense shelling by Russian forces.

The pattern is quite simple: as soon as the power station starts operating and smoke appears, Russia immediately begins shelling the facility. Despite this, the brave power station workers continue to work until the very last possible moment, but Russia nevertheless destroys vital parts of the plant. Ultimately, the plant ceases operations. A forced evacuation of personnel and equipment begins.

Strange as it may sound, history recalls similar moments from the past: in 1941, the plant was also forcibly evacuated, but on that occasion the evacuation was to the east – far from Nazi Germany. Today, the evacuation is in the opposite direction – away from the imperial invaders from Russia.

A play about the relationships between children and parents and how they change, just like music, fashion and ideals throughout the ages… whilst only one thing never changes – LOVE.

‘ALL YOU NEED IS LOVE’ – an entire generation lived by this mantra... And so begins the story told by Mike Bartlett’s play – with the Beatles’ song ‘All You Need Is Love’, with cannabis, the rejection of parental authority, a liberal sex life, discussions about the Vietnam War – but without politics or moralising, and, of course, three young people – Kenneth (Simeon Damyanov), his brother Henry (Asen Kobilarov) and Sandra (Eli Koleva). The action takes place in the remarkable year of 1967, preceding the student unrest that revolutionised and changed the world – it is probably no coincidence that the characters are students at Oxford.

The production by the Bulgarian Army Theatre follows the love story of Kenneth and Sarah, recounting their journey from the late 1960s to the present day. And although, through their children – Rosie (Bernarda Bereanu) and Jamie (Tigran Torosyan), Mike Bartlett levels accusations at the entire ‘flower power’ generation, which has cast a shadow over all subsequent generations, in director Krasimir Spasov’s production no judgements are passed, yet no one is innocent either.

‘Till Death Do Us Part’ is a production based on a play by Doug Wright, which explores the themes of defending personal freedom and human survival in a world of successive inhumane dictatorships. Through fragments of the life of Charlotte von Malsdorf, who lived in Berlin during the Second World War and subsequently under the communist regime in East Berlin, Doug Wright – who is also a character in his own play – attempts to piece together the complex puzzle that is the fate of the contradictory figure of Charlotte. At times, he loses himself in his thrilling journey towards his muse. A journey reminiscent of falling ecstatically in love. And one that will ultimately leave behind a beautiful declaration of love for all time.

Duration: 90 mins.

5fe7cc38a27b779f1d1500e223ae4f4c63fa1141.en:
In the 1930s, the Soviet Union was ruled autocratically and uncompromisingly by Joseph Stalin, whilst the state apparatus cracked down ever more ruthlessly on anyone with a dissenting opinion. In this atmosphere of persecution, oppression and violence, Mikhail Bulgakov wrote one of the greatest novels in the history of world literature – *The Master and Margarita*. It was not until 40 years later that this future classic, beloved by generations, was published in its entirety – decades after Bulgakov’s death.

Today, the questions that *The Master and Margarita* poses to society and to each of us remain as relevant, pressing and unanswerable as ever. The play *The Master and Margarita* is a time capsule, thanks to which we can experience the magic that Mikhail Bulgakov creates in his universe, where the fates of ordinary people intertwine the Devil and his impressive retinue, Pontius Pilate and Jesus Christ, as well as two lovers and their true, faithful, eternal love – the Master and Margarita Nikolaevna.

62714226e7ac4da6d98027d09326df3ecc576ac9.en: ‘LOVERTIGO’ is a self-deprecating comedy-drama about the fear of love and the chaos we create in our own lives. Inspired by the relay-style structure of the plot, the title intertwines love and vertigo — that emotional dizziness we all experience from time to time. The play poses painfully honest questions: What do we do to ourselves? Why do we keep love at arm’s length? What is the price of our own foolishness? And why are we so often afraid of happiness itself? ‘Love-Dizziness’ is a story about people who run away from the chance to be happy, because they know how fleeting and fragile that moment is. Laughter, self-deprecation and emotional clashes intertwine in a production that reminds us how difficult it is to allow ourselves to love — and how very human that is.

62c8d1f42b7f7eb5599cc99d34f09456f3508ebf.en:
But, as is always the case with Shakespeare, this whole romantic description turned out to be a great pretence. In fact, *Much Ado About Nothing* is a play about the impossibility of love happening, being realised, or being told.

“Much Ado About Nothing’ is not an aphorism that, with a mischievous smile, resolves petty romantic misunderstandings, but a metaphor for the futile efforts of human beings to find themselves in a hostile and chaotic world.”

Krasimir Spasov

For 400 years now ‘Much Ado About Nothing’ has been captivating and infecting audiences with its bold, youthful allure and the intoxication of love, whilst not sparing us the pain and disillusionment when that intoxication sheds its deceptive, frivolous mask. The comedy rises to a philosophical understanding of human nature and love, and never ceases to thrill audiences.

The song from the production *Paradise* is emblematic of Stefan Valdobrev and his work as a singer and composer.

Four close friends meet up one late summer evening to have some fun in the town park. Just as before, they start outwitting, outtricking and outtalking one another. And from one laugh to the next, from one curious observation to the next, the world around them transforms into another, magical reality. And in that world, anything is possible – you can wish to fly on a magic carpet, or meet a firefly that will take you home to visit. Anything is possible when we keep our true friends in our hearts!

This is the play’s premiere.

648eb1b25c488f3f69bd118cb8da999b83cbd90a.en:
What is infidelity? And what about betrayal? Can love conquer all? And where does salvation lie?

​Rosa and Nick are facing their most serious family conflict yet, but it will be put on hold when, on a rainy Sunday evening, Stella unexpectedly turns up at their door. Where is she headed? What is her secret?

Zahari Karabashliev

Fragments of a foreign world reach us, which we reconstruct, reorganise and recreate as best we can, often in the hope of finding some meaning. I do not think, however, that these days we go ‘to the theatre’ to seek meaning. No drama — whether written, performed or lived, and no matter how harrowing — has taught us anything. So why do we continue to go ‘to the theatre’? Why do we find entertainment in other people’s crises? To forget who we are? To remind ourselves who we are? Or to feel alive again?”

Zahari Karabashliev

Working on this play has robbed me of the certainty that I know enough about human relationships. In fact, every talented work of art shakes our confidence in such knowledge. I’m glad that *Sunday Evening* did just that, raising new questions and new doubts for me.

It’s well worth watching for the love, the struggle for love and its consequences.

6580fa2e58b8c4cab26fc4a1299de0cb7a7edb72.en:
I can’t remember when I first came to love Sagan’s writing. As I grew up as a reader, she was already a ‘star from my dad’s day’. Her novels struck me as sentimental, slightly clichéd and hard to tell apart from one another. Still, they were never boring. I couldn’t quite grasp what was so scandalous about *Bonjour Tristesse*, though; I found what I was learning about Sagan’s own life far more interesting. Drugs, gambling, car crashes, scandalous relationships with men and women, heated arguments at the Cannes Film Festival when she was chair of the jury… In the few photographs of her that appeared in our press, one could increasingly see an ageing woman with an uncertain gaze, somewhat reminiscent of a weary bird…

Gradually, I began to realise just how much courage Sagan possessed as a writer. She speaks of love with the simplicity and unpredictability inherent in the emotion itself. On sex – without pretension, yet without excess; on break-ups – without tears, yet with a ruthless ‘survey’ of the wounds. The heyday of her literary fame may be behind her, but Sagan remains among those authors who will be there for us when we face our defeats. Facing the fading summer and the loneliness that follows.

I cannot remember when I first came to love Sagan’s writing, but I know why. Because of her ability to guide us in the art of embracing sadness. And to do so with a smile. Almost.

65a150100e2627d09f39791a9cb3af61a2666ece.en:
If you’ve had enough of it all – including the big issues, the petty concerns, and even yourselves – do come along to the play *Three Versions of Life*. Yasmina Reza’s exceptional script will offer you ways out of this predicament.

If you haven’t yet grown tired of humanity and the universe, do come along anyway – this play might just be tailor-made for you.

Yasmina Reza’s plays are modern classics. Audiences continue to pack the theatres because, much like Oscar Wilde, she manages to address the most compelling human issues with a brilliant sense of humour and incisive irony. In *Three Versions of Life*, it’s the same again – the audience can laugh until they cry at the story of two families and their squabbles, which cover everything from whether you can eat after brushing your teeth to whether galactic glows are flat. Some time ago, Hollywood studios decided to release *Oppenheimer* and *Barbie* on the same day, encouraging audiences to watch both films at once. If you missed out on the ‘Barbieheimer’ experience, *Three Versions of Life* offers you the same opportunity.

65c13f28c65aa926ebca725feed03a79b9f595c4.en:
The comical plot of *CAFÉ WITH PRETENTIONS* takes us back to Sofia in 1966, to the flat of Milcho (Yulian Vergov) – a 43-year-old head of an advertising agency. We find him there with his ‘mate’ – 43-year-old Milko (Ivan Radoev). Frenzied preparations are underway in anticipation of two ladies, whom they chatted up by chance earlier in the day, for a coffee on Rakovska Street... The advice from Milcho, who is far more experienced in the art of seduction, almost gives Milko a boost of confidence; although an architect, he has taken his career as far as the coveted post of ‘head of technical documentation at the office’, is utterly inexperienced when it comes to women. At the height of their preparations, their third friend – 43-year-old Minko (Monyu Monev), a research assistant specialising in Old Bulgarian – arrives at the flat uninvited. His secret desire is to escape the ‘cosy family life’ into whose shackles he has recently fallen, and to have a drink with his friends. This evening and its unexpected denouement give rise to a host of absurd and comical situations. A meeting that, at first glance, seems unpretentious, yet is full of pretension.

‘CAFÉ WITH PRETENTION’ was not Georgi Markov’s original title. The comedy was first published in 1965 by the Committee for Culture as ‘We, the Stray Cats’ – the title under which the play was first staged at the ‘Trudov Front’ Theatre, starring the actor Yuri Yakovlev. Unfortunately, the theatre closed that same year and the premiere never took place. In 1966, in the magazine *Theatre Library*, Georgi Markov’s play was published under the title *A CAFÉ WITH PRETENTIONS*.

67263259e7ddafbff0d404df1b8b08531ce5d803.en: “Jumpy” is a contemporary English play by April de Angelis. With insight and plenty of humour, the author depicts the relationships between parents in their fifties and their children in their late teens. Nominated for the prestigious Laurence Olivier Award, the play offers a rare opportunity for vivid performances in which the comic and the dramatic intertwine, whilst the extremes are not exaggerated, as they stem authentically from life itself. As dynamic and grotesquely funny as our own times, the story touches and moves the audience, speaking with resourceful candour and unexpected tenderness about love, sex, upbringing, care, youth, ageing, perspective, aimlessness and hope.

6802e64fbfb969e8772f8e8b98babea1c1fb8955.en:
More than half a year ago, I read *A Treatise on Sneezing* – Boyan Kracholov’s second collection of short stories. I read it in one go, and straight afterwards – for a second time – I reread his earlier work, *A Church of Dreams*; I met up with Boyan, and over the summer I read many more of his texts – short prose pieces and plays – which he sent me... This was followed by several meetings – now of a working nature – prompted by the sudden, powerful impulse to ‘bring to life’ on stage these vivid, intelligent, meaningful, poetic and self-deprecating pieces – in fact, more monologues than short stories – which ‘cry out for the theatre’.

Monologues by a 33-year-old man, a man at the age of Christ, who mercilessly examines himself and the world in search of meaning. Who has nowhere to escape from the curse of his intuition regarding his destiny. An intuition about existence. A man who writes – and creates – in order to discover.

If Boyan’s claim is true – that his writing is inspired by the theatrical experiments of ‘SFUMATO’ – it is even truer that what he writes now inspires new theatrical ideas. What kind of theatre is encoded in these texts – we discovered this during the workshop ‘Despite the Deepening Darkness’ held in January. It is with curiosity and enthusiasm that we invite you to the performance we have created together!

699ea689f83a32145cacd0003edf1c44963a6f22.en: HAVEN’T YOU EVER WISHED, at least once in your life, NOT TO HAVE TO PAY? Well, today you don’t have to pay! For nothing – that is, for everything… You can take whatever you like from the shop. Word of this spreads through the neighbourhood and people flock to the supermarket in droves. But… What would you choose if you only had a single chance to take it without paying, and would it even be in the supermarket? If it isn’t there, what would you replace it with? A ‘philosophical’ question about the meaning of ownership… That’s my biggest mistake as a director – I imagine I’m turning something shallow into something profound. That’s not the case here; the show is quite entertaining and doesn’t weigh you down with heavy metaphors. Will the ‘buyers’ pay for what they’ve nicked, or for the fact that they didn’t take it for free? You’ll find out in one of my funniest shows, brilliantly performed by some of the funniest artists I’ve ever worked with. And what will the police, sent to arrest the robbers, do? Will they ‘clamp down’ on them, or will they side with them? Come and see for yourselves!

6c80a20b083158bc7505b0abb246fc91280f5eab.en:
Four little girls are sitting on the hill overlooking the Laurelton Oaks estate, dreaming of getting married there. Four young women at their school-leavers’ ball, without boyfriends but with a bottle of whisky, vow that they will find true love and be each other’s bridesmaids, no matter what happens in their lives. Thirty years later, they continue to honour that vow. Whether it’s one of their second or third weddings, no matter where they have to travel from, regardless of the season, their busy schedules or personal setbacks…

‘Bridesmaids Forever’ by the successful writing trio Jones, Hope and Uton has been described by critics as a ‘feel-good play’. Probably because, despite all the twists and turns in the characters’ lives, it is really about friendship. It’s about how far you’re prepared to go to keep a promise to a friend. The answer is provided by these four determined yet indecisive, sensitive, vulnerable, brave and loyal women. Their story will touch anyone who has ever been moved to tears by the modern classic *Four Weddings and a Funeral*. Together with these wonderful actresses, we have endeavoured to transform this ‘happy play’ into an elegant, entertaining theatrical production.

A man, at the height of his career, encounters four very different women – sentimental and ruthless, familiar and unfamiliar at the same time – and, together with them, ‘dances’ on the edge of the unlived. And he draws us into unravelling a great mystery – whether he is a Don Quixote of love or an ‘emotional assassin’.

In contrast to the ‘typical’ hotel rooms where these encounters with the past take place, the women chosen from the ‘love list’ are very different and unexpected. What else does the writer hope to learn from his schoolgirl love, Sam, played by the wonderfully multifaceted STEFANIA KOLEVA, whom we remember and love for her unique roles in theatre and film? What drives him to rediscover the extravagant, headstrong and uninhibited Tyler? In this role, we’ll see a surprising transformation by ILIANA KOJABASHEVA. The encounter with Lindsay, the beautiful lady with an enduring charm, played by BOYKA VELKOVA, is a real test for Ivan Yurukov’s character. But his emotional world will prove most vulnerable in his clash with Bob, whose complex nature is portrayed with impressive precision by ANA PAPADOPOULOU.

6eb92537116f020a04b0b14b9995a6ccd1436b68.en:
St. L. Kostov’s *Golemanov* is one of the most popular Bulgarian plays. Written almost 100 years ago, it appears time and time again on the theatre bill. Audiences seem to know what they’re going to see, yet they go to see it again. This is surely because a good comedy – in this case, political satire – confronts them with a theme that is ever-present in their lives, but from its humorous side. And who doesn’t like to laugh?

The aim we set ourselves with our production is for this laughter not to be the mockery of an outside observer, but to turn everyone’s gaze inwards, and for irony to become self-irony, because the pursuit of power is inherent in human nature; it motivates our actions and guides us. Where it leads us is a matter of maturity and preserved purity.

That is why we do not judge the characters, but look to them in the hope of understanding them, so that we may understand ourselves. Laughter helps us to discover and accept the truth more easily; it purifies and heals.

The talented puppeteer Geppetto is a true artist! With love and skill, he creates the son of his dreams from a strange, playful piece of wood. He names him Pinocchio, and he turns out to be a character in his own right. A real ‘wooden head’ – headstrong, restless, curious and so naive that he cannot tell right from wrong.

Children are supposed to go to school, but Pinocchio simply won’t have any of it… He runs away and sets off on his difficult journey as a wandering wooden boy, getting into all sorts of trouble. Pinocchio longs to be a real boy and, through his adventures, discovers what it means to be alive. He realises the power of love. He experiences the magic of kindness. His guardian – the Blue-Haired Fairy – also reveals to him some unpleasant and shameful traits of character – such as lying. A faithful talking cricket accompanies him and advises him in times of danger, of which there are many.

The Wonderful Adventures of Pinocchio is a thrilling tale of ‘becoming human’, which the Italian writer Carlo Collodi told more than 140 years ago.

Did the mischievous Pinocchio become a real boy? Let’s experience his adventures together – AT THE THEATRE!

70ec406701d789f4143a425b5ee82a0cfd46aaba.en: This is a play that pokes fun at clichés – the clichés of love at first sight, and indeed at second and third sight. It also pokes fun at marriage rituals, whether held in civil registry offices or in church. And at the reasons for getting married, too. A good-natured mockery of traditional family values, as well as of generally accepted human norms, takes centre stage. The performance pokes fun at homophobia, but also at its cause – homosexuality. It has the audacity to mock violence. Why? To render it powerless. It reminds us that senseless cruelty has, in fact, no reason and ought not to exist. All these things are justified by a sort of ‘Americanisation’ of humanity. In our case, a strong dose of ‘Balkanisation’ accompanies this Americanisation. Can we laugh at cruelty and primitiveness? Yes! We’ll survive simply because we’ll laugh. I know from experience that a smile disarms. My desire, and that of the performers, is for the violence in the production to have a certain ‘Tarantino-esque’ flavour, combined with a dose of ‘Marx Brothers’-style comedy. We also ask the question: where is the world heading, and how far has it gone… ‘Where on earth are we heading?’, as Radičkov would say. I would say ‘through the rye’, so that I might finally pose the ‘clever’ closing question: is there a Saviour in the rye? You’ll have to see for yourselves. Come and see us! Let’s hope the end of the show doesn’t coincide with the end of our world, ha ha ha!

71aba4d53ac3d44b32cce5281cabf0abca3bebfe.en: The film depicts the turbulent life of Rosa Balistreri – a legendary figure in 20th-century Sicilian folk music. She was not merely a singer, but a cantastorie – a storyteller through songs that carry a powerful social message. Her distinctive, husky and dramatic voice became a trademark and a symbol of Sicily. Steeped in melancholy, the songs of the ‘Sicilian Rose’ give voice to pain, social oppression, emigration, poverty, the tragic fate of women and an indomitable spirit. For this reason, she is often regarded as a singer of social rebellion. Ignazio Butita, one of the most influential Sicilian poets of the last century, described her as ‘the Soprano of the South’.

‘Disaster’ means a major, devastating calamity or catastrophe that affects many people or an entire community, but it can also refer to a great social scourge, such as love.

So, on that note, don’t tell me that when a man falls in love he becomes even stronger, even braver… blah, blah. A man in love is disoriented, giddy, timid, helpless. And women aren’t any better! Love confuses them, throws them off balance, makes them act foolishly, blinds them… in short, it’s a hopeless business. And when two lovers meet, or – God forbid – four… Well, that’s a disaster. An uncontrollable, genuine disaster. An unpredictable, erupting volcano. But so what if we know that? We’ll never give up on love, on that captivating, mad magic! Live this life with a smile and don’t give it a second thought! Trust in love, come what may!

7381c0f338d59f3f784f4f17a2b25489ba99814f.en:
Even when it tackles serious themes, the theatre provides us with entertainment and gives us pleasure. There are lower and higher forms of entertainment — the theatre encompasses both. There is lesser and greater pleasure — the latter stems from great drama; it is richer and has greater impact.

So writes Bertolt Brecht, the author of the play *Mother Courage and Her Children*, and he himself demonstrates that even the most dramatic plot can be staged in such a way that the audience is entertained whilst at the same time actively reflecting on the events brought to life under the stage lights.

The hardships of war, but also its benefits; the tranquillity of peace, but also its complacency; care for others, but also their innate selfishness; the lofty human dream, but also the degradation of humanity; the freedom to choose, yet the deliberate renunciation of it — in *Mother Courage and Her Children*, these conflicts seek their resolution.

A deeply moving theatrical experience, based on a play by Bertolt Brecht.

75eee2c200380cca29567529d79c3184bd0ad5d8.en:
‘The eye never gets used to the dark’ is a line from the memorable production *Roots*, directed by Leon Daniel, which opened the newly established Sofia Theatre 60 years ago. I still remember its poetic power and to this day I follow its legacy. I follow the spirit of theatre, which is meant to shake people – both on stage and in the auditorium – with the truth, to unsettle them and awaken their consciousness. To move us, but also to challenge us to think.

For years afterwards, the explosive intellectual and critical energy of a group of artists brought together by no mere coincidence – Yordan Radichkov, Ivan Radoev, Stefan Tsanev, Konstantin Iliev, Valeri Petrov, Ivan Peichev, Boyan Papazov, Veselin Hanchev, Georgi Markov, Parvan Stefanov, Leon Daniel, Lyuben Groys, Nikolay Polyakov and a group of magnificent actors, supported by directors capable of taking risks – was creating, within the constraints of the socialist context, a theatre of the future. Bold, provocative, talented and ahead of its time.

It was astonishing how, in spite of the context, the dream of a different kind of theatre – a different intuition about existence in art and its mission – was becoming a reality.

For us – the next generations of theatre practitioners – the lessons of this theatre were both a source of courage and a test.

Our performance today is an inspired attempt to take up the ‘baton’ from them and carry it forward – not to the letter, but in spirit.

765efe5f807784ee608093baf443bf974f715567.en:
Yordan Radichkov’s *Lazaritsa* takes us into a world that resembles our own, yet is not quite the same. At the centre is Lazar — a man who thinks he’s been through the mill, but hasn’t yet realised exactly what has happened to him. Everything seems like a game that oscillates between the funny and the sad, but a game in which the rules change on the fly, without much regard for what’s what.

Situations get tangled up like yarn in a cat’s paws, slightly absurd; conversations veer off in unexpected directions, and laughter pops up exactly where you least expect it. Beneath the surface, however, something is constantly stirring and won’t leave you in peace.

In this performance, even the sounds are born before the audience’s very eyes and ears. The sound of footsteps, the animals, the storm – everything happens here and now, as part of the play, as if the world itself were being reassembled on stage.

‘Lazaritsa’ is like a conversation by the fire, which starts as a joke but gradually makes you listen more closely. And just when you think you’ve understood everything, it turns out that perhaps you’re only just getting started. And as is often the case with Radichkov — the more you watch, the less certain you are about what is true and what is simply an entertaining story. Or perhaps that is precisely what makes it so fascinating.

If marriage is an adventure, then this French play is a comical journey through life’s greatest mysteries. Namely, the relationships between men and women.

A wedding disaster will spark a series of reflections and give rise to clever strategies for marriage and love. Misunderstandings, absurd interpretations and impossible ideas will bring the three characters together in their chaotic attempts to bring back a runaway bride.

Flawless dialogue, improvisation and audience interaction make the play not only funny, but also immerse the audience in the bewildering reality of modern relationships.

As in *Desperate Husbands*, the humour is sharp, engaging and often draws the audience into the fun. And once again, the music is provided by Dimitar Zahariev on the guitar.

Here, the chairs are made to measure. The porridge doesn’t burn, and the bears are well fed… most of the time. But your stories – they’re always in safe hands.

‘You’re the script’ means that nobody knows in advance where the evening will take us – not even us.

‘You’re the script’ means that you’re welcome exactly as you are.

Perhaps tonight is the very moment to tell it.

The performance is based on real stories from the audience and takes place in a safe, sharing atmosphere. Your stories are spontaneously re-enacted by the actors and musicians on stage. ‘To play it back’ – to bring the story back to life, acted out. To see it from the other side.

The new season of The Story Hunters is beginning; we’re turning a new, still-blank page.

We warmly invite you to share a special time together, seeking answers to questions both big and small.

79e5c48556187b051a0a2e339a0caa6448c1fcbd.en:
You, the reader of these lines, are not just a spectator! You have the unique chance to be the screenwriter and director of what you are about to see. What is it? “Scissor-Slayer”!

Imagine you’re in a cosy hairdressing salon where a murder takes place. The victim? A famous pianist. Suspects? Everyone – from the flamboyant hairdresser and his flirtatious assistant to the lady and the antique dealer, even the police. Each of them has a motive, but there is only one culprit. An investigation begins, in which you too can take part and decide how this crime mystery will be solved.

In ‘Scissors-Smasher’, you’re not just a spectator, but a detective. Join the investigation, question the characters and help solve the crime. “Scissor-Smasher” is a unique comedy that never repeats itself, because the plot takes a different turn every time, thanks to you – the audience.

“Scissors-Slasher” has been seen by 2,000,000 people and has broken audience attendance records in Bulgaria with nearly 400 performances on stage at the “Bulgarian Army” Theatre. For 20 years now, this crime comedy has continued to garner rave reviews and make even the most sceptical audience members laugh.

Treat yourself to plenty of laughs with the crime comedy “The Scissor-Slayer” – a show that is never quite the same, thanks to the audience!

The result is ‘A Story of Passion’ – a fusion of theatre and flamenco, reality and imagination, in which the two embark on the adventures of Don Quixote and Sancho, swap roles, sing, dance and draw the audience into their madcap performance.

The original music by Nikolay Ivanov (OM), winner of the ‘Ikar’ and ‘Asker’ awards for theatre music and composer of scores for over 55 films, intertwines with the raw, passionate voice of Carlos Otero. Asya Ivanova also joins in the live singing, whilst dance and theatre transform ‘A Story of Passion’ into a captivating musical and theatrical experience, brimming with humour, passion and unexpected twists.

7cd75b77a7a798e56477a59b7317ca424b38dc6b.en:
‘Tales from Times Long Past’ by Rudyard Kipling – that is the title we have given to our story, which will take you to the mouth of the Great and Majestic, the muddy-green Limpopo River, then on to the unexplored tropical territories along the shores of the Red Sea, and finally ending by the languid waters of the Vagay River, somewhere in Central Europe.

Join us on this intercontinental journey to discover why elephants have long trunks, with which they can scratch not only their ears but even their backs; why rhinoceroses remain ill-mannered to this very day, staring at you insolently with their narrow, pig-like eyes; and—is it even possible for a self-respecting primitive man from the Tevar tribe and the most disobedient daughter, raised by the warlike women of the Tegumai tribe, to understand one another and reach an agreement?

Treat yourself to a magical morning filled with laughter, songs and, above all, lots and lots of imagination! Oh, yes, we almost forgot: a gift for all our loyal viewers is a must!

7e301a26e304138acea3ed6105c5f7bc042aedec.en:
The play *A Midsummer Night’s Dream* is a journey between love and illusion. A world in which the boundaries between reality and fantasy become blurred.

In her interpretation of this magical comedy, director Diana Dobreva creates a visually captivating production in which the classic text is combined with poetic imagery, contemporary aesthetics and music to reveal the timeless themes of love, desire and the bewildering human world.

The forest comes to life, elves and fairies whisper forgotten truths, whilst the characters – lost in love triangles and tangled passions – search for themselves in a dream that is more real than reality. The fantastical does not shy away from the dramatic; rather, through humour, human vulnerability is revealed.

‘A Midsummer Night’s Dream’ is a play about the power of imagination and dreams set against reality and the law. The play is like a faceted sphere, offering different mirrored perspectives and endless interpretations.

The visible flirts with the invisible, the real with illusion, dreams with nightmares, order with chaos, desire with love.

The main action of the play takes place in the woods near Athens.

The forest as a place where one can escape the law, a place where the unconscious and the subconscious can be set free and where hidden desires and passions can run wild.

That is why our forest in the production is different; the stage space is more like a labyrinth of the subconscious, or as Shakespeare says in the play, ‘…merely a dream-like jumble in your head’.”

7efd2a04c886df8afe114cbdb282ece465fcc7c9.en:
What can we say? When? How? Under what circumstances?

Although we take freedom of speech for granted, there are things that can no longer be said. Especially in relationships between men and women.

Yet they tell each other everything. Two characters with hellish personalities. He is unscrupulous, provocative and never holds his tongue. She is unfiltered, cheeky and arrogant. They love each other, but spend most of their time arguing and clashing. Money, politics, cosmetic surgery, social media… The topics are endless, as is the argument, because neither of them will back down from their position.

7fea71e1d5fe9ab3eff6713118f5a44096a3d41c.en:
What are the dimensions of social media’s influence on artists, and what happens when everyone who presents themselves online is an artist? How is the contemporary dance scene changing in this age of manuals and recycling?

This is a performance that will reinvent itself and its foundations each time, consuming, revise and reference what has gone before, whilst its performers will be in a constant state of confusion as to what and how they should focus their attention in order to make it work.

This is, by its very nature, a doomed format, because it will not be filmed and you will only be able to watch it live!

The performance explores understandings of and approaches to contemporary dance – and dance in general – in the context of rapidly changing trends, easy access to information whose content is determined by market principles, the need to save time and achieve quick results, as well as the sadness that everything has already been invented.

80269c3eb69659530640524eee17258f5173bcad.en: Keiko has been an odd one since she was a child. Every action she takes is governed by her own logic, which, however, does not fit into the overall framework of society, whose rules she cannot comprehend. That is why she decides to withdraw into herself and mimic the behaviour of those around her, so as to be ‘normal’ rather than an ‘outsider’. At the age of 18, she starts working in a konbini and discovers her own little slice of paradise. Conbini are shops in Japan where you can find everything, round the clock. They are all alike; the staff wear uniforms and the service is standardised, with rehearsed and masterfully executed phrases for customers. Within this perfectly functioning mechanism, Keiko speaks and acts exactly as is expected of her. For her, being a cog in the convenience shop machine is not merely a means of survival, but an ideal way of life.

80375601765cbf8af3dbebeb1f13e84f4a04ef0b.en:
Three couples. A completely innocent misunderstanding. And one evening when all secrets will come to light, an evening when all relationships will be put to their most dangerous test – the truth – so that they may grow stronger and love may prevail. ‘UNSAFE RELATIONSHIPS’ is a comedy about those evenings when love, jealousy, passion and fear sit down at the same table – and everyone talks at once. “UNSAFE RELATIONSHIPS” is a comedy that strips away inhibitions along with the clothes. A comedy of desires, in which the line between love and jealousy, passion and fear, a kiss and a gunshot is as thin as lace. Here there are no safe words, no safe glances – there are bodies that desire one another and hearts that are afraid.

The most dangerous relationship is the one you didn’t dare to start.

And the safest is the one in which you have enough courage to love – and to forgive.

820865c782a230e2f955bc2df865f153a2483379.en:
How is the story of Hamlet possible? Our answer is that it is possible as a fairy tale – ONCE UPON A TIME…

That is why we neither tie ourselves to the period in which the play was written, nor do we seek the specific historical parameters of the events described, nor do we set the action in our own time. We believe that, in this case, the essence is revealed if we answer the question ‘when’ with ‘once upon a time’, where this fairy-tale ‘once upon a time’ means ‘always’. This approach allows us to experience a truth that transcends the limitations of specific contexts and the interpretations tied to them.

‘HAMLET’ is one of the most famous plays in the world. No doubt many of you have heard its bloody tale of the young prince who encountered a ghost, ‘went mad’, and posed the universal question ‘To be or not to be?’, the answer to which is still being sought today. He killed and was killed, along with all those caught up in his refusal to understand why fate had chosen for all this to happen. And here we are today – once again faced with this brilliant text, immersing ourselves in the breathtaking world of Shakespeare’s language and, with the utmost sincerity, attempting to reveal to you the answer to Hamlet’s question.

And so… whilst our story is drawing to a close, that of our poet is not. For his monument is eternal – not carved in stone, but woven from verses, and he will be remembered… as long as words are born of breath, and breath of life!

82e184aae48c60b2114b44555a7a31d5e8a36ba7.en: The play *An Enemy of the People* by Henrik Ibsen, the founder of modern drama, has taken on new significance and a fresh context in Europe in recent years. Combining elements of a political thriller and a family drama, it raises the intractable issue of the lack of freedom and truth in a democratic society. ‘An Enemy of the People’ explores the age-old theme of the individual versus the system, but set against the backdrop of a world of post-truth, media manipulation and humanity’s relentless pursuit of economic progress. ‘Public Enemy’ is also a solitary cry for a fresh start for civilisation amidst the now barely distinguishable simulacrum between truth and lies, between knowledge and the apparent benefit to society. Or, as Guy Debord, quoted in the production, says: ‘Society has officially declared itself to be a society of the spectacle. To be famous outside the realm of the spectacle now means to be known as a public enemy.’

82f1aef11401bd4c8326782cf921d0b65eb5c7f3.en: The film focuses on the lives of Jean and Corinne Lucher – a father and daughter in occupied France. She is a young film star, whilst he is a powerful media magnate and a friend of Otto Abetz, the influential Nazi ambassador in Paris. The story is told from the perspective of Corinne, once hailed as ‘the new Garbo’. As she records her thoughts on a borrowed tape recorder, she tries to reconcile her unwavering love for her father with the fact that he was executed for treason in 1946. Despite its impressive running time of over three hours, *Lights and Shadows* attracted more than 300,000 cinema-goers in France in the first week after its release alone. The film also sparked a heated debate regarding the Vichy regime. Whilst many critics from the centre and the right praised it as a masterpiece that captures the historical nuances, left-wing publications such as L’Humanité have criticised it for downplaying the actions of those who voluntarily served the Nazi killing machine right to the very end. Laurent Joly – a leading French historian specialising in the Vichy regime and state anti-Semitism – has praised the film for its ‘ambiguity’ and ‘duplicity’. According to Joly, “it was not pacifism that drove Luchère towards collaboration, but his venality and lack of morals”. ‘Light and Shadow’ is a harrowing reflection on moral compromises, cruelty, valour and all that remains in our lives against the backdrop of major historical upheavals. Rather than overwhelming the viewer with raw emotion, Xavier Giannoli unfolds the story with patience and delicacy. Silence is part of the narrative language, whilst the contrast between light and shadow serves as a subtle metaphor for memory, absence and the fragile resilience of human bonds. The cinematography in *Rays and Shadows* is never an end in itself or merely decorative – it serves the film’s emotional core. The actors’ performances are restrained and precise, devoid of theatricality. Every gesture feels authentic and dramaturgically justified. If you’re looking for a conventional plot or instant gratification, this isn’t the film for you. But if you’re ready for something more contemplative and introspective – something that resonates rather than forcing its message upon you – *Rays and Shadows* will offer you an exceptionally rewarding experience. A film of rare sensitivity, in which the invisible is just as important as the visible. (anonymous viewer review)

A lack of empathy, superficial charm and high self-esteem are just some of the traits that can characterise both a serial killer and the most successful manager.

It is therefore no surprise that the ideas of a Swedish psychologist, adapted by the Spanish playwright Jordi Galceran, have been so warmly received by audiences.

In one of his latest productions, director Plamen Panev created his own adaptation of the text and invited Nikolay Urumov, Asen Blatechki, Svetlana and Hristo Bonin to join the cast of this comedy, which is a quirky blend of psychological thriller, crime drama, intellectual puzzle and reality TV show.

The brilliant comedy *The Dirty Bastard* is a play focusing on the brutal relationship between big business and the little man, who is prepared to sacrifice his morals for the sake of his career and a good salary.

A production packed with plenty of intrigue, plenty of surprising twists, plenty of laughter, entertainment and a variety of characters. And the audience have the chance to join in by guessing how it will end – who is the mole?

85cf781d81de766731a03be710caa7a7099e1d1a.en:
Patricia Highsmith’s novels are the sort that, once you’ve opened them, you read in one go. It is also said that they are addictive. One of her admirers was none other than the master of suspense, Alfred Hitchcock, who adapted her book of the same name into the cinematic masterpiece *Strangers on a Train*. *The Talented Mr Ripley* is another of Highsmith’s bestsellers, which has become a cult film. She is undoubtedly one of the most psychologically perceptive authors in the world of crime fiction. Although horrified by her stories, we find the criminal’s path along which she leads us irresistible.

Our production introduces you to Patricia Highsmith at a time when she was already living as a recluse in Switzerland and had no intention of publishing any more novels. An enigmatic young editor arrives at her home, sent by her publishers to persuade her to write one more story about the charismatic criminal Tom Ripley. What follows is unexpected, chilling and astonishing… But we cannot reveal any more here. You must see the production, and you are sure to be captivated by the world of the talented, eccentric and utterly magnetic Miss Patricia Highsmith.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

8640a28c964a2f31063177d8affefccc1679af6c.en:
‘Stories’ is a play by one of the most interesting contemporary British playwrights – Nina Raine – which has never before been staged in Bulgaria. Set within the genre of contemporary tragicomedy, the play explores an important issue for modern Europeans – the problem of reproduction – not only in its biological sense, but primarily in its socio-existential context. Is the individual truly disappearing? And why does the grand narrative of one’s life fragment into a multitude of smaller ones?

At the centre of the action is Anna – a woman in her late thirties who dreams of becoming a mother. After her long-term relationship breaks down and her hopes of a traditional family are shaken, she decides to take her fate into her own hands and find a way to have a child without a permanent partner. Thus begins a series of unusual, comical and sometimes painful encounters with various men, which reveal not only the contradictions in modern relationships, but also societal attitudes towards women, the biological clock and the right to personal choice.

Anna is a casting director who is conducting the most important auditions of her life – in search of a father for her future baby. And so the story of her personal film turns out to be a quest for its own plot and meaning. ‘Stories’ is also a play about all the narratives that modern people invent to save themselves from loneliness and a lack of meaning.
8640a28c964a2f31063177d8affefccc1679af6c.src: „Истории“ (“Stories”) е непоставяна досега в България пиеса

8673b60b5515a3a29e8663abc550abe0b426308f.en:
One class, Year 11 ‘A’, has been gathering traditionally for years now with their teacher, Comrade Peeva, who is now 90 years old. They always meet at Sylvia’s small, cosy restaurant; she is generous and takes a heartfelt part in their increasingly sombre celebration. The passage of time has robbed the characters of their youth and altered their destinies, yet it has also preserved their small, unique and spirited community; which is why getting together once a year is such an important, irreplaceable experience for them. They are bound together by their devoted determination to remain united in their differences. Unexpected memories surface, long-suppressed conflicts erupt, and the jealousy between two of the female characters – who once kissed the same boy – creeps in, unabated over the decades...

What will happen at the final reunion, attended by just eight of the former pupils? Will secrets of love and betrayal be revealed? Or perhaps an unexpected visit – from friends, from ill-wishers, or simply from thugs? Will malice, cruelty or a smile prevail? What radiance does life hold at the end of the road? And you’ll discover the answers – delivered with sadness, laughter and music – in Nedyalko Yordanov’s latest play, *As It Is*, thanks to the cast of brilliant actors we’ve come to know over the years.

8753fdad842f595785ef8ff1d94a09d98591a4f7.en:
‘Kazimir and Caroline’ is a play by the Austrian playwright Eydön von Horvath – one of the most significant German-speaking authors, who left a profound mark on the development of modern drama and the theatrical heritage. The action unfolds against the backdrop of the festive Oktoberfest in Munich – a place of merriment and mass revelry, which contrasts with the inner emptiness and loneliness of the characters. The play explores the transformations of love under the influence of socio-economic upheavals, crises in human relationships and the loss of identity. Its motto – ‘and love never stops’ – sets the tone for thinking about social connections as a bittersweet carnival of life, an endless whirlwind of instability, breakdowns and new hopes.

Horvat depicts a world in which social insecurity shakes the foundations of people’s personal worlds and stirs up human fears of losing ground – the fear of falling off the social ladder and ending up in realms of loneliness, cold and despair. These fears determine human choices and actions and transform relationships into a fragile, illusory, unstable or pragmatically instrumentalised reality. Whilst Oktoberfest glitters with lights and boisterous ecstasy, the characters’ inner worlds remain fragmented and troubled. Thus, the play transforms the festival into a metaphor for a society intoxicated by apparent prosperity, yet ravaged by inequalities, fears and a lack of human closeness.

8785006f38eef8c9ba8c0ee031344ed731fb08d7.en: In a mountainous region from which most young people have emigrated to Europe, Reggio is the only craftsman in the village who takes care of everything. Whether it’s repairs, building work or some minor everyday task, everyone turns to him… ‘Everyone Calls Him Reggio’ is a Balkan tale that takes us through the amusing, unpredictable and sometimes absurd misadventures of the local hero – a man with golden hands and a kind heart. A story brimming with humour and human warmth, which reveals the unique idyll and rebellious spirit of a place cut off from the wider world – where time seems to have stood still, yet life continues to buzz with activity.

What is it? A theatre production, a social satire, a play on contradictions, a celebration of one’s own ruins? Or perhaps none of the above?

“The Zipper of This FCKNG World: a very bad cabaret’ is a chaotic journey in which a Swiss Venus and a Balkan Dionysus meet – a comic duo trying to come to terms with the extent of their own privilege. Juggling genres, the characters frantically try to hold together the world crumbling around them.

But don’t worry – none of this is really that serious.

This is a show that won’t tell you anything.

88741037bd9e8d413d80a8a9aabf019e4c467582.en: A construction worker, a Bulgarian emigrant in Vienna, dies suddenly. His wife is determined to give him a fitting send-off and invites his closest friends to spend the night with her, keeping vigil over the deceased. Under the influence of alcohol, the vigil gradually turns into a Dionysian mystery in which the dead come back to life and the living begin to resemble the dead. The boundaries between the art of living and the art of dying gradually blur. ‘Taxi to Heaven’ follows three intertwined stories: the story of an illegal night-time wake in Vienna; the story of two employees at a funeral parlour specialising in transporting the remains of Bulgarian emigrants back to their homeland; and the story of a Polish criminal who must be smuggled across the border in a coffin.

8915f268ab66c36246d0584320bac560de3991e9.en:
One of the brightest names in contemporary jazz – the Japanese trumpeter, composer and producer Takuya Kuroda – is set to give his first concert in Sofia!

Born in Kobe, Japan, and having made his mark on the New York scene, the musician successfully blurs the boundaries between jazz, funk, post-bop, hip-hop and neo-soul, establishing himself as one of the most influential figures of the new generation.

The audience in Sofia will have the opportunity to hear live music from his latest, eighth studio album, ‘Everyday’ (2025) – a project in which Kuroda reaches new heights in his quest for the perfect balance between modern production and organic live performance. At the heart of the album lies the groove – that vibrant rhythmic energy which transforms his concerts into an experience that transcends traditional notions of jazz.

His distinctive, clear trumpet tone, combined with the use of a Rhodes piano and synthesisers, creates a soundscape where the influences of Herbie Hancock, Robert Glasper and Thundercat, yet always through Kuroda’s own artistic lens.

He has been developing his career in the US for over two decades now. Following his studies at The New School in New York, he has worked with groups such as DJ Premier’s Badder Band and Akoya Afrobeat, and has recorded for prestigious labels such as Blue Note and Concord. His name is invariably associated with the artists who have shaped the new face of the contemporary black music scene.

8a818ead7c59f5b69d32da81ff1ef0c67b672528.en:
If you wake up on Sunday after a Friday night out, it means the party was epic. No one knows this better than Filip Bukov, Pavel Ivanov, Hristo Padev, Stoyan Doichev and Skiller, for whom ‘Friday night’ turns straight into ‘Sunday morning’. The new original show reunites the four actors with the beatbox master in this sequel to the comedy dedicated to the much-dreamed-of Friday night.

The five of them cleverly skip over Saturday and glide into the calm waters of Sunday. And nothing can disrupt the serene flow of their weekend, except… that enigmatic, yet deeply unsettling, conclusion to Friday night. Having sown the seed of doubt, it shatters their dream of peace and quiet on their day off and turns Sunday into a minefield of shameful memories and conjecture.

The three Magrat sisters are back together in their hometown of Hazelhurst, in the US state of Mississippi, for the first time in many years...

Lennie — the eldest sister (Yaroslava Pavlova) — has never left Hazelhurst; she looks after her cantankerous grandfather. Meg — the middle sister (Raya Peeva) — left home to pursue a singing career in California, but so far has found happiness only at the bottom of a whisky bottle, whilst Babe (Mila Lyutskanova) — the youngest sister — has just been arrested for shooting her husband, Zachary Botrel.

Under the scorching rays of the Mississippi sun, past but unforgettable relationships and memories resurface, and each sister must come to terms with the consequences of her own ‘crimes of the heart’.

Locked away alone in the claustrophobic confines of his music room, he alternates between identifying with his instrument and distancing himself from it, searching for his true self somewhere in the space between these two extremes. He seeks it in a paradoxical and comical way. The play is a rich and varied score for a soloist and a double bass, for a person and an instrument, for an actor and an object. ‘Svirka’ is a comedy one-man show, conceived and written by Ivan Stanchev. The play is inspired by real-life stories of Bulgarian football referees and explores the choices a football referee makes throughout their career. The show draws parallels with a person’s personal life and the responsibility each of us has to be the referee of our own lives.

What is it that motivates us to blow the whistle, both on the football pitch and in life?

8cb31721a472c50c79372cbf3098aef2f540bf97.en: Fuyuko is a professional proofreader who lives a secluded life; she rarely goes out during the day, but loves to go for walks late at night, when ‘only half the world remains’. One evening she meets Mitsuzuka, a physics lecturer, as reserved and meticulous as she is. Soon the two begin to have midnight conversations as lonely companions. Like two people in a shared orbit. But can their relationship survive the cold light of day? The film tells the story of a woman experiencing her first love, but alongside the beauty of romance, it also explores the contradictions, paradoxes and deceptions inherent in human nature. A timeless love story, born of the imagination of Miéko Kawakami, author of the novels *Sky* and *Breasts and Eggs*. Her book *All the Lovers in the Night* (2011) became a genuine international sensation – it was also the first Japanese novel to be shortlisted for the National Book Critics Circle Award in the US. Yukiko Sode has established herself as one of the most exciting new voices in contemporary Japanese cinema. (International Cinephile Society)

8d8072396fba48efa3888747671cbef1511684b8.en: The production of the play *Mr Kolpert* by the German playwright David Gieselman explores the distortion of modern man within the banality of everyday life. In his frantic attempt to recapture a sense of life within himself, man is led not towards closeness, but towards total alienation; not towards meaning, but towards madness born of a lack of meaning. A tale of the end of human sensitivity and the beginning of its reification.

8dff4b3fcdb578ee93da85d089a8f9c2848452af.en:
‘Waiting for Godot’ is a play about the disintegration of identity, about the impossibility of remaining the same person even whilst waiting.

The characters exist in a world where roles, bodies and relationships shift. Memory is unstable, personality is conditional, and time is a closed circle. The second act does not repeat the first, but deconstructs and rewrites it before the audience’s eyes.

Through post-dramatic stage language, shifts in identity and a rethinking of the actor’s presence, the production poses the question: if everything can be replaced, what actually remains of a person?

Perhaps only an attempt at a painful and absurd exploration of existence itself.

911e47223e5784d81341112d525ad82af89cb281.en: #NotI is an experimental one-woman show incorporating elements of performance art, video and sound design. The story follows a woman in isolation who is trying to piece her life back together whilst confronting her own past. She is her own judge – she accuses herself, searches for where she went wrong and recreates her ‘living diary’ to rediscover her lost femininity. Rediscovering her voice, she pours out a torrent of words and feelings – some meaningful, others seemingly chaotic. In this Beckettian universe of fragmented stories, the final task falls to the viewer: to piece together the puzzle and reconstruct the story.

913476c9a86002306dff9ab4d974555a7ec51196.en: ‘Sing well, live well, die well’ – this is the motto that the opera prima donna Carlotta Berlumy has followed throughout her life and career. And it seems she has truly managed to live up to it: blessed with a naturally beautiful voice, she won a competition at the age of 17, and by the age of twenty she was already singing in *Aida* at La Scala in Milan. Life has been generous to her – showering her with talent, loyal admirers and numerous lovers. But the emergence of another opera star seemed to cast a shadow over her triumphant march across the opera stages – Maria Callas. When she first met her, Carlotta failed to recognise the threat posed by the ambitious Greek woman. Later, however, she began to see the malevolent influence of Callas in every professional and romantic setback she suffered. Her rival is her complete opposite: with a voice like a ‘fire-engine siren’, her innovative stage presence, and her model-like appearance. But the most inexplicable thing is the behaviour of the audience – the spectators admire Carlotta, but some prefer to watch Callas and boo her, rather than listen to Berlumy. Callas’s failure arouses greater interest than Berlumi’s triumph. What is the key to this mystery? What is the magic with which Callas manages to captivate crowds all over the world? Carlotta Berlumi seeks to answer these questions in the twilight of her days, when all that remains for her is to fulfil the final part of her motto – ‘a good death’.

917a0d468dddec2fcf16d4b38a325baa8c65f6cb.en:
Valeri Petrov transforms Dumas’s classic plot into a ‘playground’ for words, rhymes and stunts.

Everything on stage happens ‘as if by chance’, yet with complete sincerity. We return to the pure form of theatrical play, in which horses exist only in the actors’ imagination, and the enemy is merely a figment of the imagination.

It all comes down to just how far the actors’ inventiveness can take them.

Our musketeers are not unattainable superheroes, but entirely ordinary people – vulnerable, sensitive, very witty, and sometimes a little naïve. They are not preoccupied with existential questions, and nothing human is alien to them.

‘One for all, all for one’ is not an empty phrase, but the bond between four distinct and unique characters who, were they not so, would not have stood the test of time for a century and a half.

An exploration of the concept of ‘honour’ in a world full of intrigue (but presented lightly and without moralising).

Good always finds a way to triumph, even through a smile.

Why should I waste an hour of my life watching

‘Honourable Musketeer’ by Valeri Petrov?

Because it offers entertainment for all ages.

Because it restores the joy of pure, unadulterated theatrical action.

Because it teaches us not to take ourselves too seriously.

‘The Honest Musketeer’ is a celebration of the imagination, in which the most powerful weapon is not the sword, but a witty remark!

91e044ac7ae57c3630abcf646d0fcb7388702428.en:
Reading Talev is an immense pleasure; staging his work is an immense challenge, one that does not necessarily guarantee success.

And yet, it would be a good thing if you succeeded, even if only to touch upon his humanity, his love for his homeland, the pride he feels in his unity with the people who gave him life, and the trials he endured whilst devoting all his creative energy to them.

The lighting of the ‘iron lamp’ dispels the darkness in the souls of his heroes, awakening national self-awareness and a thirst for life, freedom and creativity.

That is why today, when the nation is shaken by contradictions, when it is melting away like a candle and living with the thought of survival, burdened by the feeling that everything is falling apart, that our children are abandoning us, and who knows what else… it is precisely today that there is no more fitting author and no more necessary title for the theatre to present as a message to its audience.

91e2bc8791c82c8093149274b9574cb517287861.en:
Years ago, the remarkably talented artist Kolyo Karamfilov told me that ‘the face is the seal of God’. Bergman is a poet of the human face – ‘the other face’, the invisible one, withdrawn into the shadow of the personality, quivering beneath the surface of apparent composure, worn down by patience, ecstatically having lost its balance. In *Autumn Sonata*, the hidden face, in the guises of mother and daughter, emerges to shift the focus away from the superficial, to shatter the deceptive veneer of everyday life and to transform daily existence into being. This nocturnal face is born of dreams, filled with passions, wounded, furious, frenzied. Yet within this face, religious hope shines through. In *Autumn Sonata*, Bergman does not point to salvation, but reveals the longing for it. The drama lies in the experience of mercy as an event, rather than as an outcome.

It is the very human striving for mercy that transforms *Autumn Sonata* into an existential event with the impact of an ancient tragedy – at once *Medea* and *Electra*.

9202af212fd41d82f1257cfc8d5c36dd0dac720b.en: Inspired by the poem ‘Whale Nation’ by the English poet Heathcote Williams, the film treats us to superb footage of whales, filmed in the four corners of the globe. Focusing in particular on the songs of these giant mammals, with humpback whales as the main protagonists, the film’s approach is initially classic, but soon offers an inventive perspective. The visual beauty, the narrative and the wonderful music (the director’s decision to ‘shake the dust off’ the rhythm of documentary cinema, shifting from pop to jazz), draw the audience’s attention to the important theme of wildlife, which we are, willingly or unwillingly, ruining and destroying, even though it is essential to human survival.

9746e76ce7ea834ccf5d49486ab95de15216390e.en:
“The Slingshot” is a play about love – about first love and last love, about great love and forbidden love, about the one true love and the impossible love.

It is a play about coming of age and about “life as a dream”.

976d80cd5ca92e62b225c397385a20f02afd82a6.en: Everything in this comical yet dramatic story begins with the appearance of a stray balloon, which had broken away from the battlefields of the Second World War and suddenly appeared above the hamlets of Avramovo. This event leads to the formation of four groups of villagers who set off in pursuit of the balloon. The characters of the pursuers are more than colourful: Teacher Kiro, Hadji Avram, Petleto, Iliiko, Matey the Good-for-Nothing, Avram the Seamster, Igoto, Pavel, Petar, Avramovitsa, Avramcheto, Babina Dushitsa. Radichkov writes of his play: ‘Also taking part in the events are: a child’s kite, a flea, a tame crow named Momo, angels carrying the soul of a deceased man from Avram’s neighbourhood, a group from Wallachia with Hutsul flutes, a group of Serbs with Arnaut flutes, a group of Greeks playing a mournful melody on stringed instruments, a group of Turks with a hodja, playing zurlas and maanetas, and the dust they raise. These four groups are meant to symbolise the Balkans, which do not remain indifferent to the appearance of the wandering balloon. Highest amongst the Balkans is our group of pursuers, as we are at the very centre of the peninsula. The Balkans are the home of eagles, the home of flying ideas; there, the human spirit soars high in the clouds, and every one of the characters has flown in their dreams at least once. This chronicle has the modest aim of showing how, from real events, the common people create myths. All myths are created by the common people, a mixture of imagination and ignorance, and a constant dream of breaking free from a wretched and despised earthly life. As it is illuminated and warmed by the human soul, this despised and wretched life begins to sound almost balladic and shines with a purely human light.”

980b5a6ad11aa65f3b23404288d053153d47b72d.en:
‘The Minister’s Wife’ was written by Branislav Nušić in 1931, in the midst of the Great Depression. A context from which the Balkans, for a host of historical, cultural and geopolitical reasons, seem as though they will never escape. It’s always a crisis, there’s never enough, we’re always screwed and bitter. At least we’re not ugly. And we’re hardly dirty. Or so we think. And we’re always dreaming that, God willing, we’ll lead our father’s brigade and sort out the country. And in ‘no time at all’. What other nations, under different circumstances, have achieved over a century, we do in a ‘five-year plan’. And we end up like a dog in a field. Just like that. A complete shambles.

Our heroine, the Minister’s Wife, wakes up one day as if in a dream, her knickers still in tatters, and whilst she’s wondering how to make ends meet, the irony of chance spits her out into the ministerial backwaters. And so the same old story about the ladder begins…

98168b336670875e3250c2c831acd4d447e7aabd.en:
"Nothing Is as We Think It Is" is Iva Sveshtarova’s latest production, inspired by the paradoxical figure of St. Wilgefortis – a bearded saint, crucified and later ‘erased’ from history.

Through the female body, the crucifixion and the miracle, the performance explores how images are created, how we ascribe meaning to them and how we come to believe in them. How an image is repeated, transformed and even erased, whilst traces and meaning remain that we continue to recognise. It seems that one and the same event can have many faces, and what we remember is not always what actually happened.

The improvisation characteristic of Durang, both as a writer and as an actor, is embedded in the play, which takes familiar everyday situations and stereotypical notions as its starting point, only to subvert or build upon them in unpredictable ways.

98a3072f4008bd060b3b2188a9cd989f76fd6f39.en: ‘The Permanent Wife’ is a brilliant example of a spicy comedy of intrigue, centred on an inevitable love triangle. The plot unfolds at a rapid pace, filled with unexpected twists and even more surprising turns that provoke genuine amazement and hearty laughter. But behind it all lies Somerset Maugham’s unsettling sense that modern man – well-dressed, well-fed and living in luxurious homes – falls into the trap of his own illusions, in the snare of his own selfishness, for the sake of which he is prepared to sacrifice everything – love, spontaneity, sincerity and even his moral integrity.
