98af8b3388d33bf4bde1aae9187b08bac4744aa5.en:
Over two evenings, devoted respectively to the themes of identity and love, third-year students from Group B, under the artistic direction of Prof. Dr Atanas Atanasov, shared their feelings and thoughts in the form of theatrical essays, structured around the principle of group storytelling.

Who am I? Where do the thoughts in my head come from? Do I have an authentic personality, or is it all just stories that my parents, friends, society, films, TV series and social media have instilled in me so that they can interact with me more comfortably?

Do I really love, or is it all just hormonal surges that I rationalise with lofty ideals and noble intentions? Do we love our friends? Even when we hate them? And our parents, when there’s no understanding between us? And what if the whole idea of romantic love is simply mass psychosis?

These and many other questions deeply move the students, and they use the medium of theatre to share their reflections with you.

Can we understand ourselves? Do we want to understand ourselves? Yes, but we just have to forget about ourselves. The attempts continue, even when we’re crying or laughing our heads off. But the hardest thing is to stand up and admit it to ourselves. Yes, we admit it to ourselves, especially in the bathroom, but when it comes to admitting it to other people, we grit our teeth and stay silent.

And it takes a lot of smiles and applause to get us to speak up.

Let’s have a laugh together and help each other out.

9a5f894a2fad113d63c1b44a12093efaa53a88b1.en:
Three friends. One unpredictable English football match. Three different bets. And a lot at stake.

Paun, Bule and Pixie have been friends since childhood, and football betting is their great passion and favourite escape from reality. This time, however, each has staked everything on a different outcome. With every passing minute, the tension mounts, the result takes a turn – and with it, so do their relationships.

‘Don’t Bet on the English!’ is a raucous, daring and painfully funny Serbian comedy about friendship, addictions and the eternal boys who wait for the last-minute winning goal instead of changing the game themselves. Because sometimes you think you’re betting on a single match. But in fact, you’ve bet everything.

9b06cfcf0e5a38e7314ba19b0c30b01716ca9c39.en:
‘BLACK COMEDY’? It probably sounds familiar to you, doesn’t it? Yes, even if you haven’t seen Peter Shaffer’s play, you’ve certainly heard of it. And now you have the chance to see it on stage at the “BULGARIAN ARMY” Theatre.

“BLACK COMEDY” is regarded as one of the funniest comedies written in the second half of the 20th century. Right from its premiere at the National Theatre in London in 1965, the production became a real hit and soon won over audiences all over the world.

‘BLACK COMEDY’ is a madcap farce that unfolds… in the DARK. Yes, it is indeed the DARK that plays the leading role in this comedy. But what happens when DARKNESS is LIGHT, and light turns to darkness? The logical question, ‘What is a person capable of when they know that nobody can see them?’ lies at the heart of the mechanism that, throughout the entire performance, provokes laughter in ‘BLACK COMEDY’ at the ‘BULGARIAN ARMY’ Theatre.

A power cut, seemingly ordinary at first glance, gives rise to a host of comical situations and unexpected twists, involving an attractive young sculptor (Veselin Anchev), his future fiancée (Luizabel Nikolova), his ex-lover (Evelin Kostova), his domineering military father (Georgi Kirkalanov), a refined neighbour (Vladislav Violinov), a drunken spinster (Anastasia Ingilizova) and a wealthy millionaire patron (Monyu Monev – guest appearance). As in any good comedy, the characters in this one find themselves entangled in comical situations, whilst the misunderstandings in the DARK lead to even more hilarious confusion.
9b06cfcf0e5a38e7314ba19b0c30b01716ca9c39.src: „ЧЕРНА КОМЕДИЯ”? Сигурно ви звучи познато? Да, ако не сте гл

9b53c94bd89fc837deeee930905b1108b60d677c.en:
“LOVERTIGO” is a self-deprecating comedy-drama about the fear of love and the chaos we create in our own lives. Inspired by the relay-style structure of the plot, the title intertwines love and vertigo – that emotional dizziness we all experience from time to time.

The play poses painfully honest questions: What do we do to ourselves? Why do we keep love at arm’s length? What is the price of our own foolishness? And why are we so often afraid of happiness itself? ‘Love-Dizziness’ is a story about people who run away from the chance to be happy, because they know how fleeting and fragile that moment is. Laughter, self-deprecation and emotional clashes intertwine in a production that reminds us how difficult it is to allow ourselves to love – and how very human that is. Director Deyan Donkov presents a stage adaptation inspired by Arthur Schnitzler’s *The Round Dance of Love* and David Hare’s *The Blue Room*.

9cdf78e0f2dde1d27bd251b3195c1e7c1407239a.en:
Is there such a thing as justice, or is the end merely a matter of chance?

Who will be granted the right to live after the truth has been laid bare without compromise?

Faced with the lift, going up or down, the characters in this play will have to reveal their true selves to the very end.

Thus, with pressing questions demanding an answer from everyone in the auditorium, Éric-Emmanuel Schmitt places the audience in the role of participants in an interactive game. He piles up ‘FOR’ and ‘AGAINST’ for each of the characters, toying with their expectations like a cat with a mouse, whilst never failing to laugh at their imperfections or to marvel at their brilliant insights. The author’s brilliant style is complemented by the inexplicable logic of life, which never ceases to deliver surprises. It is no coincidence that *HOTEL BETWEEN THIS WORLD AND THE NEXT* is one of Éric-Emmanuel Schmitt’s most frequently staged plays, both internationally and here in Bulgaria. In addition to his well-known techniques, the plot keeps the audience on the edge of their seats, much like a crime film. It provokes the pursuit of a coherent logic, whilst curiosity about the plot twists is only rewarded at the very end.

9d1d129c8c2e7c88d431aef6a97c21c2ec9240c0.en: Today in Bulgaria, two scenes preserve the image of the great artist Stoycho Mazgalov. Two portraits by the artist Nikolay Yanakiev, situated 300 kilometres apart, greet viewers and whisper a story. The film’s camera gives voice to these whispers, wanders through the ‘Theatrical Labyrinth’ of his autobiographical book, captures the memories of his contemporaries and preserves their resonance.In 2006, on National Revival Day, one of those for whom Theatre and Honour stood above all else passed away. Twenty years later, in the sanctuary of his life, on the stage of the ‘Tears and Laughter’ Theatre, we shall applaud him once more with the premiere of Niki Shumanova’s film ‘MAZGALA – A Musketeer in the Labyrinth of Time’. 23 November will be a special evening that will never be repeated. Time will stand still in memories – as we pay tribute to a figure whose story deserves to be told.

9d62b20252ed0f1a745934d5da8e2988e34771e4.en:
Two performers, armed with a single scene — or trapped within it: a customer orders a drink from a waiter. And then things go awry.

The scene plays out again and again — with ceaseless dialogue or in complete silence — until the familiar situation begins to spiral out of control. A nightmarish spiral or a grotesque farce? Roles and power dynamics are constantly reversed, until we no longer know who is the target and who is the attacker, who is serving and who is being served.

Directed by Tim Echels, artistic director of Forced Entertainment, and created in collaboration with the brilliant performing duo Bert and Nasi, ‘L’Addition’ constructs a complex, entertaining and explosive performance from simple elements. The three of them play with both the mechanisms of theatre and power dynamics — but in the end, someone still has to foot the bill.

a0f881e01f378c574829317b3493ca1d703cc676.en:
We wanted to stage a vaudeville or farce that would be as daring as a conceptual work of art.

Two friends meet in Sofia. One says to the other: ‘Do you know the difference between an installation and a performance?’ ‘No,’ replies the other…

Why Chekhov and Müller? Whilst we were rehearsing Chekhov’s *The Story of an Unknown Man* with the Russian director Anatoly Vasilyev, we analysed at length the structural links between Heiner Müller’s *Medea* and certain female characters in Chekhov’s works: Nina in *The Seagull*, Sofia in *Platonov* and Zinaida in *The Story*… Whilst working on *Bear-Hamletmachine*, I wanted to explore this unexpected similarity in greater depth.

What are the connections with Bulgaria and with *Sfumato*? *Hamletmachine* was written partly in Bulgaria and recorded in a school notebook entitled *bulgarian notebook*. At that time, Heiner Müller was living with Ginka Cholakova, whom Margarita Mladenova and Ivan Dobchev knew well.

Can a person be dead and at the same time not dead? Yes, says Popova in *The Bear*. Yes, say Ophelia and Müller in *Hamletmachine* – dead and not dead, like Nastasia Filippovna, whose footsteps can still be heard in the corridor in Dostoevsky’s *The Idiot* – a work that is so important to the poetics of *Sfumato*.

The theatre is a laboratory, but resurrection is like a farce.

a69f8c8df979f5b282bfb264dbc3bd7e095f5e2e.en:
At the end of the 19th century, Oscar Wilde was one of London’s most dazzling figures – a writer, poet, playwright and public figure, a witty aesthete and scandalous bohemian, whilst his plays were performed to unprecedented acclaim. His openness and bold personal freedom clashed with the hypocritical morality of the era and caused a storm in a society which, behind the mask of morality, concealed its deep-seated intolerance. He steps down from the glittering theatre stages and literary circles and is sentenced to two years’ imprisonment by those who, until recently, had applauded him.

The production is based on Oscar Wilde’s final work, *De Profundis*, written whilst in solitary confinement. It is at once a letter to his beloved, Wilde’s account of the final years of his life, and a spiritual testament. In it, he redefines love and betrayal, suffering and humility, and the meaning of life when all else has been destroyed. He finds strength in art as his sole refuge and in the right to remain true to himself. In this way, he transforms his personal pain into a message to the world. By speaking openly about the past and acknowledging his mistakes, he paves a path through the pain for those who have lost everything.

In a society where we are often confronted with prejudice, social stereotypes and invisible shackles, art and personal truth are a means of preserving human dignity. His confession from prison is not merely a record of one man’s fate, but a warning – that no community is free when it oppresses those who are different.

a6cd63cc12e48a5d1b731413e9713fdd76413f6b.en:
Perhaps the telephone, as a phenomenon in our lives, harbours a great danger, namely that it can easily tempt us to entrust it with our secrets, yet offers no guarantee whatsoever that they will be kept safe and secure.

A person is like a magical casket of secrets, and these secrets may be precious pearls, or they may turn out to be unseen misfortunes or cruel weapons.

A person is a Pandora’s box with several layers. And we must be able to take responsibility for our curiosity and its consequences when we decide to open it. It is an illusion to think we know someone, even the person closest to us. We cannot fully know anyone, just as it is impossible to know the universe in its entirety.”

a6cd8a645016d09056ca54bf17cdbe483b2a53d4.en:
Three women. Three perspectives. No pretence that we have all the answers. A touch of self-deprecation, a few truths and plenty of reasons to have a laugh at the things that usually send us into a panic.

Krasimira will discuss the things that will never change in Bulgaria – the queues at the Road Traffic Police, the wait at the counter for an ID card. She’ll also daydream about the same thing that wiped out the dinosaurs 68 million years ago taking us out too.

Olya Malinova will talk about what it’s like to be a ‘failed mother’, why it’s OK to love money, and who her favourite figure from the Liberation is.

Elisaveta Belobradova will talk about open communication, personal boundaries and the madness we all have. Some of us have it in greater doses than others.

a6d6e3982189360cacc13077d33facbf92c33be9.en: During an uprising in Paris, a double of Louis XIV takes his place in the palace. The young king is entrusted to the care of the musketeer and poet Cyrano de Bergerac. The travelling theatre troupe led by Madeleine Béjart serves as a refuge for the future Sun King; the actor and budding playwright Molière has only just joined the troupe, unaware of the identity of the troupe’s newest member. Cyrano begins writing a daring play for the troupe, whilst at the same time attempting to rein in the whims of the arrogant and awkward young monarch. Bursting with ideas, Molière transforms the play with wit and sincerity, unleashing his comic genius. And whilst his secret feelings for Madeleine grow ever more intense, Louis discovers the joy of the theatre and the power of friendship. Meanwhile, a conspiracy is brewing in Paris… Will the young king manage to return in time to take the reins of government?

a80ae6df80908b77265b529e77d7e69821835221.en: A young judge signs a registration document for a dubious joint-stock company. This fact remains hidden from the public, but it manages to send shockwaves through the afterlife. Shortly after signing the document that would pave the way for the unpunished felling of six thousand decares of forest in the Balkans, the judge suddenly dies whilst searching for hidden gold in the courtyard of an old landlord’s house. In the afterlife, several Bulgarian national heroes gather to call the newcomer to account. Finding himself in a position where he is to be judged and held accountable for his earthly deeds, the judge plucks up his courage, goes on the offensive, summons authoritative witnesses and, with their help, begins to judge his judges himself. The mutual judgement system of the afterlife begins to buckle under the weight of the surging old and new sins, long-standing passions and unquelled demons, deeply buried and unconfessed personal and national secrets.

a85e462b73ee29877f4804d97330ead142774f8f.en:
Somewhere at the end of the world, a hotel is rocked by dizzying emotions and comical situations.

‘Provincial Anecdotes’ is a play brimming with intrigue, doubts, confessions, a nasty hangover, fear, ignorance, careerism, passion – and all of this under the roof of a single hotel! Can all this really happen in one place and to the very same people? Yes! If they’re inside – and deep inside, with both feet firmly planted in Vampilov’s anecdotal world!

And now there’s no boundary between actors and audience. What is theatre and what is reality – the absurd infidelities, the unfulfilled ambitions, the reckless drunkenness, the ignorance worthy of pity, the distrust of selfless kindness? Is it really possible that all this is our life?

Fate mocks the characters, drawing them into its game – ridiculous and amusing, intriguing and instructive, sincere and naïve, but above all, thrilling!

What happens when desire seeps beneath the skin to become destiny? When beauty cannot be touched, yet never ceases to captivate?

The production explores human nature – from instinct to the quest for equality with the power of God. This is the story of a man who has discovered his nightmares and dreams in his passion for a woman, for her sensuality and for the impossibility of ever fully possessing her.

The atmosphere of the production is shaped by a poetic yet tense narrative exploring the human yearning for perfection. For the desire to touch the divine. Of human loneliness. Of power, obsession and the dangerous illusion that beauty can be captured, preserved and possessed.

‘With the Scent of Blue Plums’ is a performance about a person lost in their own desire to transform beauty into eternity.

adc19c6a4934a7b7149aa912384a1b55c7f2e53c.en: ‘The Room of Pleasure is Empty’ is constructed from documentary fragments and original texts by the team. The performance is the result of a two-year laboratory process exploring the inner landscape of the human psyche in relation to the Terrifying. The realm of the unconscious becomes the subject of on-stage exploration, re-enactment and staging. We invite the darkest side of the inner life onto the stage. We give voice to these encapsulated, repressed desires, which seek a way to manifest themselves in reality through distorted, manipulative and fetishised actions, in which the abuse of the body, guilt and self-humiliation lead to the unattainable depths of the human unconscious, projected into the space of the Empty Room. We stage fragments of the painful parts of our personal narratives in an attempt to re-enact the emotional legacy of our ancestors. We dramatically open four rooms – the Room of Pleasure, the Room of the Child, the Room of the Mother, and the Room of the Father – in which we explore the archetypal images from family constellations.

During the absurd encounter between the four of them, everyone starts talking about different things, but they all believe they know the truth, without realising that they aren’t talking about the same thing. af1c5fccafc8cffcc6af60d99d055a54753047ea.en: Alexei Salnikov’s novel *The Petrovs During and Around the Flu* caused a sensation in Russia in 2016, and a year later won the ‘NOS’ Critics’ Award and the ‘National Bestseller’ award. It is just as likely that the stage adaptation and director Boyan Kracholov’s production will cause a sensation. Because the seasonal flu virus, which drives the plot of the play, not only alters our perspective on everyday life but also shows that nothing is quite what we think it is, and we should not jump to conclusions about the people around us, nor about events, nor about life itself. Also because the characters in this fantasy adventure, set between reality, dreams and visions prove that there is no such thing as an ‘average person’; that, in fact, the life and daily routine of a man who considers himself insignificant and whom no one calls by his first name, a person with a dull and ordinary job, is full of wonders and skeletons in the cupboard – a life that is funny, frightening, magnificent, mysterious and astonishing.

af3e98a192125e72485fdb7018fd56184b4b2ff4.en: Court intrigues, conspiracies, the lust for power and the throne, hidden longings, fear, loneliness, love and strength. This story of the clash between two queens – Elizabeth I and Mary Stuart – has it all: a struggle for power and supremacy, self-sacrifice, betrayal and love, and the stakes are high, for this is a life-and-death struggle. One is a queen. And the other is a queen. These two queens are very much alike – both are intelligent, lonely women who dwell in their ivory towers – yet at the same time they are different. One has spent her whole life searching for love; the other sacrifices love in the name of strength. Behind the apparent battle between the two women, however, there is more to it than meets the eye. They are not fighting merely for power. They have a cause. And that is something that is sorely lacking today. Because what is power when you cannot even control yourself? Is power worth anything when you have no ideas?

b0137c4800c3156f947927d302f062268962f1bd.en:
‘NOT HUMAN’ is an introspective look at ourselves, here and now, which, with care and concern, seeks to better understand how we got to this point and, above all, how we can move forward together, guided by our most humane dreams rather than our most frenzied impulses. Weaving together fragments of Bulgarian history, quotations from famous figures and poetry, the performance delicately outlines the chaos of the things that divide us historically and culturally, and which so easily, time and again, become the basis for drawing dividing lines between us. But it also uncovers the threads of what binds us firmly and enduringly together as a community and a society.

It is precisely the theatre stage, where good dialogue is fundamental, that is the most appropriate venue for holding this urgently needed conversation within our society, torn apart by irreconcilable extremes. The opportunity to remember that the pain and anger caused by disagreement with others and a sense of injustice, are shared feelings that we all experience, regardless of what we believe, is the first step back towards us being together.

b1ce0437a0bb9b17b468630ed8d0ed5d87f35581.en:
For the twenty-year-old who has a sense of destiny and a life plan to become Byron or Christopher Columbus – ideas precede reality; by inspiration, he is a Platonist. Why, however, is it that just a few years later our future hero has already become an anti-hero, with the pressures of life weighing him down, temptations supplanting his ideas, and he falling into a state of fatherlessness, godlessness, powerlessness and meaninglessness? He shrinks; his absolute Self vanishes; his ‘image and likeness’ becomes depersonalised; and from being a creator, this ‘indefinite’ man turns into a destroyer.

This typical phenomenon – whether it be Plato, Ivanov, Andrei, Treplev or Uncle Vanya – is the focus of Chekhov’s writing from the very first major ‘draft’ of all his subsequent plays, in which we seek a living theatrical expression today. The vanishing man – the great theme, the great pain of Anton Pavlovich, which we embrace as our own today.

Prof. Margarita Mladenova

This formulation reflects our insight into the pathos that drove

the 18-year-old Antosha Chekhov to write those 220 pages, entitled ‘Fatherlessness / Without a Father / Godlessness’.

The characters in this *Godlessness* flounder amidst the remnants of the tablets bequeathed to them, which shaped the humanity within Man, from his expulsion from Paradise, through the Reformations, the Revolutions, the Nietzschean deaths of God, the spectres of Communism and Anarchism, right up to today’s liberal democracy, writhing in the agony of Permissiveness. The 18-year-old Chekhov seems to have experienced the vision of John on the island of Patmos and seen us burning.

b391ebe82197de736ec1f47316dbe32c73592ba3.en:
One encounter. One glance. One moment that changes everything.

Jean Anouilh transports the ancient myth into the 20th century – to an ordinary railway station, amidst the clatter of trains and the hustle and bustle of passengers. Two souls meet. Two hearts recognise one another. Two bodies stand still in the silence between two trains. A single fateful glance is enough to throw them into the merciless whirlwind called LOVE.

It does not arrive with a fanfare. It appears unexpectedly. It penetrates their hearts, awakening secrets, fears and desires. It takes hold of them and confronts them with the greatest trials. And all this happens in a single moment.

Two hands intertwine. Two shadows move forward. Around them, life flows at its usual pace, with recurring images of passengers, actors, waiters and cashiers. And opposite them stands the last train, yet another chance for their happiness. Hand in hand and a handful of dreams are all they need to step beyond their fear and set off on a journey from which there is no turning back.

Will love fade away in the shadow of fear?

All it takes is a single glance to find out!

What if a prisoner, acquitted after a wrongful conviction, were to suddenly return to his ex-wife? What if, having nowhere else to go, he asks to live in the flat, which he partly owns and which she shares with her new husband? What if the new husband shows understanding and says he has no objection? What if her pupils (because she is a teacher) start teasing her for living with two men in (as they put it) a ‘sandwich arrangement’? What if the two men, who have unexpectedly become close, infuriate her so much that she sends them off to sleep together on the sofa, whilst she remains alone in the marital bed? What if another woman suddenly appears, bringing with her an uncontrollable fit of jealousy? And what if none of the four knows whom they love more anymore?

Come and see the brilliant comedy by the world-renowned contemporary Croatian playwright Miro Gavran.

Three of Bulgaria’s greatest comedians await you.

b78cfcec5d858d86d2920f7817cacea025315a92.en:
A curious little girl is hiding in the crown of a large tree. Beneath it, a white-bearded, good-natured old man, on his way to the sea, sits down to rest. He spots the little girl in the branches and decides to cheer her up with a magic trick. And who doesn’t love magic tricks and sorcery? We’re all captivated by them, aren’t we? Perhaps because it’s delightfully astonishing when the impossible seems easy and entirely achievable. When an object vanishes or appears before our eyes in an instant, having come or vanished into thin air – a playing card, a bouquet, a rabbit or even a violin… We probably love these tricks because they suggest that the world and life hold all manner of magic, that friendship, hope and joy are always possible, that every moment can surprise us with its magic, as long as we do not hide too stubbornly amongst the branches of our own tree.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

b8023d9805d79dfff353e74a7cae688adc82cf6e.en:
“#antitaga” is a theatre performance based on texts by the poet and playwright Stefan Ivanov. ‘#antituga’ portrays the inner world of the modern individual, deprived of successful social interactions, their absurd and dark humour, but also their powerlessness within the society and state in which they live, and their constant self-reproach for their inability to adapt to these circumstances and build their own happiness.

‘#antitaga’ is about a person searching for meaning and a way out of the labyrinth into which they have led themselves, guided by their belief that perhaps love is enough. ‘#antituga’ is about suicidal thoughts and behaviour, clinical depression, everyday ‘burnout’, psychological trauma, addictions, bad habits, a broken society, standing up for one’s civic convictions, a lack of empathy, unrequited love, chronic negativity, laughter and death. These are themes that are becoming increasingly relevant in times of war, epidemics, economic crises and social fragmentation.

‘#antisadness’ raises the question of whether and how to carry on living, whilst waging war with oneself and in search of inner and outer peace.

b9cbbc62f5ca62e7ead506440a8d6796b9b62a6b.en:
‘Arms and the Man’ is a play in three acts by the world-renowned Irish playwright Bernard Shaw, first staged in 1894 at the Avenue Theatre in London. The West End premiere of the play marked Bernard Shaw’s first commercial success, which also launched his popularity as a playwright. It is one of the Nobel laureate’s most frequently staged comedies. Through the language of comedy, the text aims to satirise public sentiments that glorify war, exposing their inherent contradictions and excessive romanticisation. It is precisely for this reason that the author chose as the play’s title a quotation from the English translation of the opening lines of Virgil’s ancient epic poem *The Aeneid*.

Initially, the characters and the setting in the play are conventional, but in his quest for realism, Bernard Shaw, on the advice of friends, decided to set the relationships and events described within the context of the recently concluded Serbian–Bulgarian War in the Balkans. Thus, the setting becomes the home of Officer Petkov in a small town near Dragoman in Bulgaria following the end of the Battle of Slivnitsa in 1885.

Chudomir Stories is the first independent production by the Milart Theatre Company. A play about the past, the present and what lies ahead. Eight stories by the great writer Chudomir come to life, performed by Stefan Milkov as various characters, each with their own personalities, in different situations, but seen through the eyes of today’s young people.

We shall take a glimpse into our past, not merely out of curiosity, but to realise that the years have left each of us with warm memories of relatives, friends, neighbours or simply good acquaintances. A single actor will present us with the colourful and intriguing spectrum of human relationships in our part of the world, through the characters of people who suddenly appear from a Bulgarian village.

Plenty of laughter, fun and a whirlwind of emotions, interwoven with the unexpected realisation that, after so many years, we still hold the same values as in days gone by.

‘I’m Staying for a While’ is a comedy-drama about unspoken words, fears and unexpected tenderness. Amidst misunderstandings and comical situations, the characters realise that forgiveness is the bravest gesture of all, and that ‘just for a while’ is all you need to carry on.

Who is ‘Don Quixote’? Are you ‘Don Quixote’? Am I? Do we still need him, or did his ideals, dreams and hopes perish centuries ago?

‘Don Quixote’ is the brave, if slightly naïve, guide who helps us immerse ourselves in a world of adventure, dreams and escape from the drudgery of everyday life. A world of battles with colossal giants, evil sorcerers, the thunderclaps of envy, and the rivers of greed. ‘Don Quixote’ is a journey in search of opportunities to perform feats of valour and attain the world’s most precious treasure – freedom – because ‘Freedom, Sancho, is at the tip of the lance!’

bbe15fd1c1ad3bcc9b3429c4d7aabad952f13e29.en:
‘HERCULES VS AUGYAS’ is a modern interpretation of the classical myth of Hercules, centred on his fifth labour, known as the cleaning of the Augean stables.

Our version, however, transports the mythological hero into the world of modern politics, absurd bureaucracy and moral social decay, and confronts him with a challenge that even for Hercules begins to seem insurmountable. He comes up against an impenetrable wall of apathy, conformism and stupidity, and gradually begins to realise that physical strength alone will get him nowhere. The play is permeated with irony, sarcasm and humour, which depict not so much the filth itself as people’s willingness to live amidst it and the absence of any moral ideal. For me, as a director, this was precisely the great provocation of this text – the question: ‘Who is today’s Hercules?’. Our Hercules turned out to be not so much a mythical hero as an ordinary person who can be great through the choices they make.

‘HERCULES VS AUGYAS’ is a production with a sharp sense of humour and an attempt to hold up a mirror to ourselves and the audience – a funny yet painfully topical piece that reminds us that the country we live in actually depends solely on us, and if we want change, then we must start with ourselves first.”

bc844323a35309b38ba3c58332351b42f801e4b7.en: A play about love and death, honour and duty, truth and lies, court intrigues and underhand schemes, the fate of the ordinary person unwittingly caught up in them, the power of the state and the power of love – all this is Friedrich Schiller’s play *Intrigue and Love*. It is also about music and art, about the obstacles to true and sincere feelings, about the trials on the path to fidelity, and many more questions, emotions and challenges facing modern man. Written in 1784, ‘Intrigue and Love’ is described by the author as a ‘civic tragedy’, which, according to the terminology of the time, means that ordinary people, rather than gods or kings, unlike the heroes of classical tragedies, are placed in a tragic situation. And it is precisely these heroes whose fate the audience has been sharing for nearly three centuries.

bd44542e3c3ff0a92424c3352963aa9226ccd30f.en:
For the next five years, Toplocentral will have the pleasure of welcoming Trigaida, alongside Ivan Shopov, to immerse us in the magic of Bulgarian folklore through a contemporary sound.

TRIGAIDA is a Bulgarian music project that weaves the rich traditions of Bulgarian folklore with the contemporary aesthetics of electronic music. Founded by Asya Pincheva (Oratnitsa, Cosmic Voices from Bulgaria), Ivan Shopov (Balkansky, Cooh) and Georgi Marinov – Jorge (Oratnitsa, Gaidi i Tupani), the trio combines their diverse musical experience into a unique and bold sound. Their debut album, *Elate* (2021), offers a fresh take on Bulgaria’s musical heritage, reimagining traditional songs and folk

motifs through the lens of electronic genres such as drum and bass, dubstep and trip hop. The album reflects the influence of contemporary jazz, world music and neoclassical music, thanks to the participation of a number of internationally renowned guest musicians, who add depth and a global flavour to the project.

Just because we adults have failed at one endeavour or another, or have come to accept the idea that ‘chasing the wind is a waste of time’, that doesn’t mean we should persuade our children to resign themselves to the same fate. Why not set off in pursuit of the wind? You might just catch up with it, and if you do – it will reward you generously. Trying to do the impossible is the very essence of discovery. We are seeing out the year in the inspiring company of three leading figures in contemporary Bulgarian design and their latest projects.

Nikol Decheva will present her work in the field of graphic design and visual communication, Daniela Kostova, co-founder of Vavakada RE, will talk about the exciting possibilities offered by recycling and circular design, whilst Nevena Shopova will share her unexpected textile interpretations of traditional motifs.

We can look forward to an evening dedicated to bold ideas, experimentation with materials and forms, and the processes behind interesting design solutions.

be7db4de43e3a6ac134e29b8f625c9e9cb7d1471.en:
We make excuses for ourselves, saying that to err is human, thereby turning the absurd into a convenient norm. We press the wrong buttons and wait for the world to sort itself out. The real problem is not that we are misled, but our fear of admitting that every mistake is our own choice.

Eight decades after Bertolt Brecht’s plays were written in defiance of the turmoil of his time, they return today, when the world has changed beyond recognition, yet the cracks within it remain the same.

‘Human Error’ is not a play about the global chaos in the world, but about how it plays out in one woman’s life and the scars left behind by this clash.

bebf837db0135efb32f81f2ec55a965725ec97c7.en:
In 1846, the world had the opportunity for the first time to read in its entirety one of the greatest novels in the history of literature – *The Count of Monte Cristo* by Alexandre Dumas (the Elder).

177 years later, this story – beloved by us all – of love, betrayal, revenge, friendship, redemption, guilt and hope becomes part of the history of Bulgarian theatre for the first time with its premiere on the stage of the ‘Nikolay Binev’ Youth Theatre.

Betrayal, love, a thirst for revenge and hope for redemption are just some of the key elements in this captivating adaptation of Alexandre Dumas père’s classic novel. Nineteenth-century France comes to life before our eyes as we follow the trials and tribulations of Edmond Dantès (Kalin Vrachanski) – a sailor unjustly accused of a crime he did not commit and sent to prison.

Dantès manages to escape and return to society, disguised as the Count of Monte Cristo, with plans to take revenge on those who betrayed him. Dantès becomes increasingly consumed by his thirst for revenge, but will this blinding desire destroy not only himself, but also his greatest love – Mercedes (Koyna Ruseva)?

bf14a2b13a95d1b5600f3e9aed14d2cb7b6c9e73.en:
A family of acquaintances from the countryside come to visit their Parisian friends, having received yet another invitation to spend their holidays together. Their hosts do everything they can to thwart the plans of these persistent intruders, but the more lies they concoct, the more they get tangled up in them. It turns out that even the best fabrications require flawless execution.

Both families are in for surprises that no one is prepared for, and each new situation adds an even sharper twist than the last.

bf2949d441789772a42ed1ebbde46170d4cf68b7.en:
The laboratory is a space for exploring the complex and mysterious world of objects and their potential to preserve memory, tell stories, unlock poetic worlds and interact with bodies and spaces.

Participants will be introduced to a wide range of techniques for observation, thinking with their hands, exploring with all the senses, seeking out the voices of objects, handling and partnering with them, reimagining their meanings, and analysing materials.

Through individual and group activities, participants will experiment with the performative potential of their own personal objects, as well as familiar and unfamiliar objects, such as a sheet of paper. The workshop is a space for discussion, reflection and sharing. Participants will gain practical experience, become familiar with key philosophical terms relating to objects, and explore the work of artists from Europe and Latin America who are developing the ‘theatre of objects’ genre. They will be provided with guidance and recommended reading so that they can explore their interest further after the workshop has ended.

At the end of the third day, we will invite a friendly audience to the cosy atmosphere of the Toplocentral bar. Each participant will present the story of an object, developed during the workshop. At the end of the event, we will present *The ‘Panoptikum’ Box* by Martina Novakova – a one-person show set in a character’s home and the first ‘auto-play’ of its kind in Bulgarian.

bf99dac3158823e87bb4190aeae2c906a6048c5f.en:
Jessica Parks is a successful judge, a successful mother and a successful wife. At one point, however, she realises that everything she has been fighting against – her greatest moral and social enemy, upon which she has built her entire success – actually turns out to be a part of herself. This conflict forms the basis of *Inter Alia* – one of the most interesting new plays of the last few years. In a style that blends humorous stand-up comedy with a courtroom-family thriller, *Inter Alia* explores the relativity of consent in heterosexual relationships, the fragility of contemporary ideologies and the difficult balance between career and family faced by the modern individual.

*Inter Alia – a legal term meaning ‘among other things’.

c03025d72fe32716b26124475833a4774ec99629.en: A bitter comedy of manners in which the director skilfully confronts both actors and audience with the question: are we, or is time, to ‘blame’? and invites everyone on a journey of self-discovery, evoking the charm of old Sofia’s high society of yesteryear, with a hint of love and theatricality, and the truth that we are all inclined to tell others only what we cannot hide. ‘The Guilty One’ is a play in which the characters often repeat: ‘That’s just how things were back then’. They utter it as an explanation, an excuse, a defence… This attempt to shift the blame for our own compromises onto the times is, in fact, a rather convenient role we play for our own sake. Except that no era is guilty enough to make us completely innocent. Dimitar Dimov wrote ‘The Guilty One’ in an era weighed down by guilt. Among its many monstrous distortions is one that we seem to have forgotten most easily: the hypocritical unquestioning manner with which we deny or disregard the unpredictable power of emotions. The characters in this story grapple with the fears, constraints, illusions and clichés of the late 1950s. ‘The Guilty One’ is a strange play, very much an outlier in Bulgarian drama, notes Yuri Dachev. With the inexplicable nature of the attraction between the characters, with the inevitable catastrophes, with the unspoken revelations. But our continuing failure to understand the division of guilt – our own and that of the times – is what makes this text vivid and contemporary.

What if the life we dream of is already happening — just somewhere without us?

Emma Bovary is constantly gripped by the fear that life in its fullness is

somewhere else, in other worlds, and the present is never enough for her.

The various possible visions cause her to constantly measure the distance between

the present and the ideal. This breeds dissatisfaction and turns the dream into not just

a dream, but a refuge — an illusory world as an escape from reality.

When does the desire for something more turn into an inability to accept

the present? What happens to a person when the life they are living turns out to be too

mediocre for the ideal they imagine?

But one fine morning, when it met the grumpy crocodile, who didn’t like questions one bit, the little elephant… suddenly found itself with a big, long nose – a trunk… How exactly did that happen, you ask? c358a14e184b0f35c75b9e671c708a36b7043742.en:
The story of ‘The Bremen Town Musicians’ comes to life on stage at the ‘Nikolay Binev’ Youth Theatre, with plenty of music, dancing, adventures, laughter and surprises galore. The animals from one of the Brothers Grimm’s most beloved fairy tales – the Donkey, the Dog, the Cat and the Rooster – familiar to children and adults alike, meet after being cast out by their owners.

Their chance encounter inspires them, and they decide to set off for Bremen, where they plan to become town musicians. Everything goes according to plan until two dangerous and fearsome robbers block their path. As for where and what Bremen is, you’ll find out at the end of the show.

c405453713449f4c45288a0f3e9d4fa694e14edd.en:
‘Night Butterflies’ is the second instalment in a documentary trilogy (‘Spiders’, ‘Night Butterflies’, ‘God’s Little Cows’) and focuses on the stories of women who provide sexual services.

The production explores the tension between personal choice, morality and social attitudes. It raises questions about the place of sex workers in Bulgaria – caught between legal changes and enduring stigma, between visibility and exclusion.

Created using VOX POPULI’s verbatim technique, the performance utilises authentic interviews, recreated word for word by the actresses. The documentary narrative unfolds as a dynamic theatrical experience featuring original choreography, music and active audience participation.

c4496cca7ef069c4e2c64d501ab57fd7702bfed2.en:
A Marriage Contract – a witty comedy of manners in which subtle satire, everyday misunderstandings and brilliant humour intertwine.

Efraim Kishon, a classic of Israeli humour, masterfully explores the themes of bureaucracy, family values and the clash between tradition and reality. At first glance, the story of the search for a lost marriage certificate seems entirely Israeli, but in fact it is universal and relatable to everyone.

The main characters are a not-so-young married couple, former kibbutzniks, who took a rather casual approach to the formalities when they got married. Now their daughter’s fiancé, a man of strict principles, is insisting on proof of the legality of their union. The bewildered parents embark on a convoluted journey, full of comical situations, through memories, disappointments and the discovery of true feelings. Arguments, nostalgia, unexpected twists and a touching reconciliation – all this makes the play not only funny, but also deeply human. Audiences can look forward to a light-hearted, dynamic and intelligent comedy, in which the laughter conceals a reflection on life, love and the question of what is more important – documents or genuine feelings.

c4aba26e6fc8ccc7c6a4988d76ce73fe12050a8e.en:
When you’re young, you believe that life owes you incredible miracles. Some of us rush headlong to seek them out, whilst others sit around waiting for them to fall into their laps. Meanwhile, you spend your days with friends, pining for partners, or wasting time on video games or fashion websites.

Our hero is just like that. But then again, not quite…

Hovhannes is right here before you. Playing the part of Hovhannes. No make-up, no pretensions, ruthlessly alone, uncompromisingly funny, endlessly curious… waiting for incredible miracles!
c4aba26e6fc8ccc7c6a4988d76ce73fe12050a8e.src: Когато си млад вярваш, че животът ти дължи невероятни чудеса

c4c39ed61ff18449503131ada0e589805a27d44e.en:
The letters from him to her, and back from her to him. Spanning an entire lifetime. A frenetic action sequence in which events, stages of life, feelings and moods unfold at astonishing speed... The film slows for a moment, painting a specific scene for us – whether naive, sad, frightening or hilariously funny – before hurtling through the gears of time towards the next. A chat whose breathless lines skip over everything trivial and insignificant to immerse us in the rich wine of a love that just can’t seem to happen and categorically refuses to die. Yana Marinova and Teodor Papazov will tell you a story that has nothing to do with you, yet in which you will never cease to recognise yourselves.

The performance is presented with the support of the National Culture Fund under the ‘Programme for the Restoration and Development of Private Cultural Organisations’.

c4ed3e15e1724b2f4081f95ab06b8b00e5ed812c.en: A film about the life and philosophy of fashion magnate Brunello Cucinelli, as seen through the eyes of Oscar-winning director Giuseppe Tornatore! How did a farmer’s son build a multi-billion-dollar luxury empire? Brunello Cucinelli is the founder of the renowned Italian fashion house specialising in luxury cashmere garments. Through documentary footage, personal recollections and dramatised scenes, the film traces his journey from his childhood in Umbria to international success, revealing his philosophy of ‘humanistic capitalism’, which is founded on human dignity, artistic mastery and social responsibility. Tornatore builds the narrative around a symbolic card game between Cuccinelli and an enigmatic opponent, who remains unidentified until the very end. Thus, the story becomes a parable about fate, time and the courage to follow one’s dreams, whilst Nicola Piovani’s music lends the film an added sense of poetry. Unconventional in form, ‘Brunello: The Visionary Gentleman’ is a true cinematic treat and yet further proof that the director of ‘Cinema Paradiso’ and *The Legend of the Pianist* is an unrivalled master of dramatic vision and epic scope in cinema.

c4fbea451ccbf6374cdf4873dc36a75c2bcef076.en: Two families spend every summer together in a magnificent chalet in the Alps. But when a seemingly harmless incident involving their daughters escalates into a shocking tragedy, their long-standing friendship is put to the test. As each couple tries to uncover the truth and save their own daughter, uncomfortable truths come to light and carefully concealed tensions escalate. The façade of respectability finally crumbles when everything they believed in as spouses, parents and friends is called into question… Is there a line you wouldn’t cross, even if the stakes were the survival of your own child? c70fa798f5996a8f27ecf44e7e95a348ebd13c99.en:
On 16 April 1925, the dome of the Cathedral of the Holy King (now known as St Nedelya) in Sofia was blown up. Over 130 people were killed. 500 were injured. As a result of the authorities’ swift crackdown, which began that very same day, over 150 people disappeared without trace in the space of just two weeks.

One of them was the journalist Yosif Herbst – the husband of Viola Karavelova, the elder sister of Lora Karavelova. And whilst Viola wanders the streets of Sofia in search of her missing husband, whilst she, through her love, tries to rise above the political antagonism that divides people solely into enemies, Bulgaria, torn apart by the tension between the government and the opposition, by a refugee crisis, famine, debt, coups, uprisings, assassinations and political murders, is going through one of its most turbulent periods.

Unfortunately, its history, though comparable in tragedy to that of its sister nation, has remained forgotten. This performance, inspired by real events, represents an attempt to rectify this oversight, as well as to trace the inevitable link between social processes and personal experiences. And to ask: Is it possible to find a way of life that excludes the very idea of an enemy?

c89d888e87370a23d5fd5e806c87631fcf84d1d7.en:
‘The Little Prince’ is a family show that skilfully brings together two worlds on stage – that of children and that of adults. The protagonist’s adventures take him to various planets, where he meets people who have lost their sense of purpose and direction – a lonely king, stargazers, a geographer, a lamplighter, a signaller…

Somewhere amongst them, he discovers love in a flower, which he comes to regard as his own, and friendship – in a fox who has long been waiting to be tamed.

c8d455de534e6783e731bccc962164268e040095.en:
This short play by Alexander Pushkin holds many mysteries – the author neither finished it, nor gave it a title, nor published it. To this day, scholars continue to debate both the genre and the structure of *The Mermaid*. Many writers and poets have attempted to complete the ending of this one-act drama about ill-fated love, betrayal and revenge. Even in the 20th century, Vladimir Nabokov could not resist this temptation, writing the play’s most famous ending. It is as though Pushkin himself had invited readers and their descendants to interpret *The Mermaid* in their own way, to let their imaginations run free, to seek new meanings, and to relate it to the present day. The young director Teodora Lilian saw Pushkin’s play not as an old fairy tale, but as a thoroughly contemporary story, performed by modern people. ‘What is happiness?’ the characters in the play seem to ask themselves – and us. Throughout the ages, people have answered this question in different ways – love, family, children, freedom, success. And throughout the ages, they have paid for their choices with their lives.

Pushkin, of course, does not know the ‘right’ answer either. He doubts, grieves and reflects alongside the audience, and indeed – as all manner of unexpected events can occur in the theatre – he may even appear amongst the characters in the play...

c9d158e2e6ea3310d12c582cfd96b57b90747486.en: How much courage does it take to swim against the tide? And how much strength does it take to follow your own path when it does not align with society’s expectations of who you should be? In 1939, on the eve of the Second World War, Swedish swimmer Sally Bauer defied social norms and expectations to achieve her goal. She was determined to become the first Scandinavian woman to swim across the English Channel. The film raises questions about motherhood and ambition, personal choice and the price of freedom. Director Frida Kempf first learnt about Sally Bauer’s story whilst reading the novel *Happy Sally* by Swedish author Sara Stridsberg, published in 2004. Initially, Kempf was under the impression that Sally Bauer was a fictional character. When she realised that she was a real person, she began to research her life and discovered a book containing Bauer’s reflections on the year leading up to her swim across the English Channel.

‘The Year of Magical Thinking’ draws you into the very heart of a personal storm. A place where pain, love and hope battle for the final say. A year in which reality and memories intertwine in an attempt to make sense of the inexplicable.

Following the global success of the book of the same name, *The Year of Magical Thinking* comes to life on stage at Theatre 199 in a powerful, intimate and deeply human theatrical experience.

The production transforms Joan Didion’s autobiographical confession into a universal tale of love, loss and that ‘magical thinking’ which helps us carry on.

The text takes the audience on a journey that is painfully candid, yet at the same time filled with unexpected hope.

Emotional. Honest. Inevitable.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

ccf5847ba157382448ac33e35c9d424738b4ab59.en:
Three women shut away in their little house near the gloomy Irish Sea. Time and again – as if in an endless game – they relive a long-gone night in the town’s dance hall. A night that seems to have become their only reality. The reality of impossible love.

This ritual is interrupted only by the unexpected appearances of an utterly absurd delivery man, who bursts into the ladies’ kitchen to bring them fish. And to recount the latest gossip circulating around the island. At first glance, his comical presence distracts the characters from their bitter memories.

But is that all there is to it? Is it possible, after all, for love to find its way to this house, so far removed from the dance hall?

‘The New Dance Hall’ marks the dazzling Bulgarian stage debut of the renowned contemporary Irish playwright Enda Walsh. The play masterfully combines explosive humour, verging on the grotesque, with unexpectedly lyrical imagery and an almost poetic language. The author constructs a new theatrical form of the theatre of the absurd, through which he specifically attacks the painful triviality of our times.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

d1046cb82c06bbfe0ee50b1db8ba20be0e76fa32.en:
In 2016, with the blessing of David Lynch and Angelo Badalamenti, Xiu Xiu released and went on tour with the surprisingly successful album *Plays the Music of Twin Peaks*. Out of respect and tribute to their favourite TV series, the band decided to postpone the 2018 concert. Following the recent and untimely passing of David Lynch, the band began receiving several high-profile requests to revive their interpretation of this iconic music. However, in their desire to always strive to follow, honour and draw inspiration from the incredibly high standard set by David Lynch, Xiu Xiu have instead delved even deeper.

ERASERHEAD XIU XIU is a new live concert accompanied by a film, which utilises field recordings, homemade instruments created specifically for the concert – an organ, modular synthesisers, vocals, torches, electrical interference and elements of concrete music to express the strange emotionality, contradictory sexuality, relentless darkness and exceptionally unsettling lunar landscape of this masterpiece.

The original sound design and music by Alan Spelt and Lynch serve as a guide for Xiu Xiu’s sonic expansion, reflecting how they were influenced by them as fans and musicians. The original film provides the visual lens through which Xiu Xiu’s work is viewed, as it is disrupted and jostled by the band’s imaginative, supplementary footage.

Is it a short-term art installation, an explosive tribute to a cinematic triumph, an epitaph to an idol, or an entirely new work? YES

Is the man a cockroach or not? In what situations are we prepared to crush another person, even if only in our imagination, where this symbolic murder can go unpunished?

This is the theme that runs through the works of Heiner Müller, F. M. Dostoevsky and Franz Kafka. The play *Poem about Cockroaches* attempts to draw parallels between these three stories about the dehumanisation of one’s neighbour and poses a challenge to its audience: And you, if you had the chance, would you take the life of someone who dares to kill with impunity?

For our creative team, theatre is a form of rebellion, albeit a tame one. It is a space in which we can imagine a different kind of justice—one that is not corrupt and can effectively identify and punish the guilty. To hand down sentences and strengthen citizens’ trust in institutions. If not in reality, then at least somewhere there must be such an ‘outlet’ for civil discontent.

Man in the trivial patriarchal world, his paths to crucifixion and the mistake that defines him: a clumsy player on uneven ground, with faltering resistance and guaranteed failure.

Life as a competition, wayward shots, pyrrhic victories, untenable supremacy, aimlessness.

The crisis in society versus the crisis in the soul.

A man with an invariably striking presence.

The story of an impressive anti-hero with a surname that renders him faceless.

Loved in the moment of his strength (by Sarah) or of his weakness (by Sasha), he is broken and (self-)isolated.

The story of each and every one of us.

‘There are thousands of Ivanovs. An utterly ordinary man, no hero at all…’ (Chekhov)

He has squandered his chances. A present yet fictitious participant in the lives of those around him.

A recurring figure in the role of the central character, towards whom everyone gravitates. A loser and, paradoxically, a favourite.

d5050d514d979bfc50869b9b8580cac0affeed63.en:
The absurdity of the times we live in makes time an even more elusive element of our existence. Where is it, when is it, what is it, does it even exist? In fairy tales, they dress it in a shirt and trousers, a moustache and a fringe. Is that what time is? It could be anything – everywhere and nowhere. It is something that is not specific, yet this lack of specificity is very precise.

In ‘TIME’, everything begins with a breath. A moment of pause, in which you take a breath and attune yourself to something that is in no hurry. The performance doesn’t draw you in abruptly, but invites you – to slow down, to listen, to feel how time unfolds. And when the journey ends, comes the exhalation. Quietly, almost imperceptibly, like the end of a circle that closes upon itself.

Our performance is like a jigsaw puzzle, made up of pieces that, at first glance, do not fit together. Fragments of time, memories, movements and sensations scattered freely. Each carries its own meaning, its own edge and shape. And only when they all come together does the whole emerge. A picture in which every part finds its place and time. There, the absurd falls into place, chaos subsides, and time ceases to be a question, becoming instead an experience.

This iconic production returns to the stage of the ‘Nikolay Binev’ Youth Theatre for the second time – half a century later! First staged at the theatre during the 1976/1977 season, *The Seagull* was directed by Mladen Kiselov.

*The Seagull* comes to life on stage – fragile, painful and mercilessly true. A story about love that doesn’t happen at the right time. Or perhaps shouldn’t happen at all. About dreams that clash with the daily struggle. About the desires we have today – but which of them will we still hold on to tomorrow? Or in 10 years’ time? About people who seek meaning – and sometimes lose it. A story about each and every one of us.

We look forward to welcoming you so that we may experience this encounter together – with the theatre, with A.P. Chekhov, with ourselves… and with all that remains unspoken in the silence, through which we often say more to one another than with all the words in the world.

Admit it, it’s a bit strange that things never turn out the way you’d like them to in your dreams. Especially if you’re a bit of a jinx. No matter how angrily you react at times like these, perhaps it’s best just to play along with the game you’re already part of. You never know – luck might just come your way at the most unexpected moment.

Mihail Tazev

I wake up. I grab a quick breakfast on the go. A battle on public transport. I rush to an address. No ‘good morning’. No ‘welcome’. Get on with it! Get a move on! Shut up! Nobody asks me who I am or what I believe in. I skip lunch. I’ve got no time. I glance up at the sky. I bump into… Someone swears at me. Second address. Risk level – 9. I’ve got no chance of defending myself if something goes wrong. Get on with it! Get a move on! Keep your mouth shut! A vicious dog attacks me. I step on a slice of pizza or some fresh… I miss the tram. I run to the third address. A jolt of electricity runs through my body. A blow with a walking stick to my wrist. If I could travel through time, right now I’d… I’ve no time to think. A girl smiles at me. Should I stop? I’ve no time. Get on with it! Work hard! Keep quiet! Last address before I collapse into bed. I’ll eat another time. I start thinking about the stars and the meaning of… I fall asleep. Tomorrow is a new day. How much can I take before I blow a fuse?

Other participants in the conference include: Alex Kovachev – founder of IDEA Studio, Ralitsa Chokhadzhieva – 3D artist at Chaos, Martin Kuvandzhiev – founder of Encorp.ai, architect Victoria Ilieva – founder and creative director of VIArchitects, architect Viktor Cholakov – co-founder of Cholakov and Gongalov Architects, Ruzha Stoykova – founder of Code Rouge, Velizar Dimitrov – founder of the contemporary design studio ROOMSTUDIO.

db81d19e489b346e3de3336cefda13086c4f22ba.en: The Puig family have seven children. The story begins with the wedding of Jacques, the youngest son. The father is not present at the event — he has been disowned by the family. The groom’s brothers and sisters, however, are delighted to be together again. But can the love between Jacques and his charming wife, Martine, heal the wounds of their childhood? A parallel storyline takes us to Tokyo, where a Chinese worker steps in to help Leyla, a Turkish woman, during a document check. This small gesture of compassion evolves into a story of alienation, migration and the difficulty of finding one’s place in a world where identity is defined by formal borders and procedures. The acclaimed French director and screenwriter Christophe Honoré has adapted his own stage play *Le Ciel de Nantes* (‘The Sky of Nantes’), which premiered in 2021. He describes the story as an artistic reimagining of memories of his own family.

Behind the scenes at a theatre, things are always endlessly fascinating. This is where thrilling performances are created; this is where the magic of the performing arts is born… But it is also a place of intrigue, rivalry and romantic entanglements. And when the actors’ behind-the-scenes passions spill over onto the stage – right before the audience’s eyes – the play and real life erupt into incredible comic chaos: forgotten lines, missing costumes, falling scenery, romantic twists and turns. At every moment,

the performance is on the brink of disaster…

The most interesting thing is that, in the end, both the audience and the actors are satisfied.

‘Noises Off’ is a witty self-parody, created with a love of the theatre and empathy for the actors’ craft.

dc655184cee75532c2d9e2f3ac3c180025c6ca12.en: Initially, the actress Paraskeva Dzhekelova suggested staging a recital based on Vazov’s love poems, and then the concept expanded, and work on this lyrical tale of love got underway with incredible dedication and passion. Vazov’s intimate poems reveal his most vulnerable side – first and foremost from an artistic perspective. Vazov began writing at the age of 19, inspired by his love for Katerina; he had not yet developed a lyrical style, no models to follow, if you will, nor any literary language, and his poems were merely a surge of emotion. Most of them were destroyed in the burning of Sopot, whilst some that survived, as well as those written later in Ruse, were included in *A May Bouquet*. Much later, as late as 1919, in his personal anthology *My Cradle Smells*, do we encounter polished, well-structured and masterful intimate poems – yet even the most successful among them do not match the power and intensity of his true masterpieces. Vazov’s intimate poems are his most vulnerable side, partly because we have, in a peculiar way, denied him this connection to the emotional, personal essence of life, and partly because he himself was more than reserved, laconic and discreet on the matter, here and there he would let slip a painful word or two to Prof. Shishmanov or in a letter. Regarding the writer’s private life, there are only conjectures, a morbid interest in his death and almost no understanding of the era, his mission, his patriarchal upbringing and the consistency of his values, which predetermined his immense, albeit tremulous with passions, infatuations and inspiration, SOLITUDE. Alone, yet united with everyone, with his people.

dc973ec31c9fc12f67ac4e930570e11e3224e464.en:
At the heart of the production lies the ancient myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, naturally re-enacted and reimagined through the sensibility and reflection of the modern individual, faced with several existential problems: war as a perpetual condition of humanity, mobilising yet also eroding its creative energy; the oblivion and (self-)deceptions to which we willingly succumb whilst fleeing from the truth; the artist’s solitude as a privilege both sought and defended; the power of love in its metaphysical and mystical dimensions.

Why does Orpheus descend into the underworld? Where, in fact, does he descend – into hell, amongst people, to Eurydice, or to his own fears and illusions? Why does he break the prophecy, turn round and look at Eurydice, knowing full well that this gesture dooms him?

dd09c423ea5bfbd919b655409889453d5286d861.en: Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira), the director of a care home for the elderly, is keen to introduce an innovative approach to institutional care, despite the reluctance of some of the staff. Based on a philosophy of empathy and mindful presence, the Humanitude approach involves listening to and respecting the personal dignity of each resident. On the verge of physical and mental exhaustion, Marie-Lou decides to attend a theatre performance to which she has been invited by chance, after helping a young boy she does not know. After the performance, she meets the Japanese director Marie (Tao Okamoto). An extraordinary friendship blossoms between the two women, bound by the idealistic aspiration ‘to make the impossible possible’. The film is a loose adaptation of the documentary book of letters *When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn*, co-written by Maoko Miyano and Maho Isono. The book bears witness to their warm friendship and mutual support. Ryusuke Hamaguchi transports this tender, intellectually stimulating and humane story to the Parisian suburbs. With his first film made outside Japan, the director demonstrates his unique gift for employing subtle emotional nuances and balancing dialogue with silence. The plot unfolds patiently, with an exceptional sensitivity to every gesture, allowing the conversations and silences to generate profound emotional power.

de98c7ebbb0ebc753ad4377b112b6bf9dac641cf.en: On 27 July 1986, Queen performed the biggest stadium concert in their history at the Nepstadion in Budapest in front of 80,000 ecstatic fans. The concert was part of the famous Magic Tour – the last tour on which the band travelled the world with their lead singer, Freddie Mercury. Three years before the fall of the Berlin Wall, this was the first concert by a Western rock band to be held in a stadium behind the Iron Curtain. The event was of such great significance to the Hungarian authorities and the film industry that a team comprising some of the country’s finest cinematographers and technical specialists was assembled to film it, ensuring the concert would be preserved for future generations.

df798fc5821a1fc1251d6ead49c8887878ac012a.en: Tired of waiting for roles that never came, one night Claude Magnier sat down and wrote a play himself, one that did justice to his talent for comedy. Thus began the career of a first-rate playwright, whose farces remain a staple of theatres and cinema screens to this day. His plays are brimming with unexpected and unpredictable situations. Just when you think the author has fired his very last bullet of originality, the plot takes a sharp turn and everything that seemed calm and safe is once again called into question. There are no positive heroes in his works. You’re already convinced you’ve worked out who the winner is, and just a moment later they’re already on the losing side, whilst those who appear to be lying defeated on the ground turn out to be holding the winning cards. The author himself admits: ‘I try to put myself in the shoes of the audience, who are wondering what will happen next. Today’s audience wants breath-taking and constantly surprising comedies. That is why the wit I put into my plays goes far beyond the ordinary.”

The performance explores the democratic rights of the body in exile, the constant crossing of borders, and the question of who has access to healthcare, a beautiful smile and a pain-free life in today’s world.

On 20 December at the Toplocentral Regional Centre for the Arts, choreographer Zhana Pencheva will present her solo piece ‘I Love It When You Look at Me’. ‘I Love It When You Look at Me’ is the result of the long-term artistic project ‘Bodies in Pleasure, Bodies That Care, Dancing Bodies’. The project explores sensibility, the performative identities embodied by the dancer, and the erotic presence of the dancing body. The performance examines the dynamics of the relationship between the body and its environment – music, gazes, other bodies, emotions, sensations and the uncertainty of the unknown.

e09798d9e8ac35bca7a15139da7723f5dd47c6f7.en:
The biting and incisive humour, delivered with intelligent irony, and his witty, rapid-fire dialogue are the hallmark of the hugely popular, prolific and multi-award-winning French screenwriter, playwright and director Éric Assous. ‘When I create my characters, I always try to show not what sets them apart from those around them, but what brings them closer to them,’ says the author, offering us a key to understanding the character development in this play, which explores, with an inevitable sense

of humour, the relationships between married couples. They are ordinary people, susceptible to temptation, tragicomic in their attempts to defend their weaknesses – far too human to be judged for them: jealousy, rivalry, the erosion of feelings, petty betrayals, awkward compromises with one’s conscience. The touch of suspense that the plot maintains right to the end, the constant twists and turns in the course of the story, and the gradation of emotions made our theatre company’s creative process both enjoyable and filled with empathy. We hope to convey this humanistic spirit from the stage to a well-meaning audience of connoisseurs of good comedy.

e10ec7369bcd6f09ca3c03fe3f621b0e792c6a0e.en: A garden, a wedding, a suicide, a monk, a hallucinating intellectual, a former actress, another woman: topoi and characters from a non-existent yet authentic play by Chekhov. A play that is a phenomenon: it foreshadows situations and motives that promise to emerge later. Here, still unformed, in their infancy, they draw us in, transport the imagination to the unease of self-knowledge, provoke and stir us. A play of insight (the simultaneity of penetration and realisation) into life as a one-act drama, allowing us to feel what is happening to us in its predetermination. And in its collapse: the passion that does not engender reciprocity, the closeness that does not lead to love. Loneliness as both an advantage and a burden. The horror of the promised Elsewhere. Existence, set in motion by light, directing our inner vision towards the darkness within us, laying bare, protecting, warning. The electricity of thought as an energy reserve, an impulse and an instinct for life-saving recharging and rebirth.

e18478848a54a8e25782e3fd5312c6c18ac6a691.en:
All the synonyms for the word ‘provocative’ apply to Michel Houellebecq’s *The Elementary Particles*. The novel, which brought him worldwide fame, exposes the problems of contemporary European society in a provocative, bold, arrogant, even offensive manner. Through the captivating stories of two brothers – a failed writer and a world-renowned biologist – the novel explores love in an age of hyper-technology. The questions are posed with brazen audacity, yet also with an idealistic vision of humanity’s future.

It is a challenge to adapt for the stage a novel so crucial to understanding the processes of our times. The team’s approach is ironic and paradoxically lyrical, in keeping with Houellebecq’s vision. Doomed to live, man effortlessly breaks with the past and is only just learning to recognise the sounds of the future.

The production is a social dystopia that raises the question of whether, in an increasingly dehumanising world, humankind retains its capacity to love. The answer is sought through a journey back and forth in time. The guides are the director (author of the stage text) and the actors, for whom Houellebecq is a key reference point in making sense of the new paradigm.

The production *The Elementary Particles* is part of the ‘Theatre+’ programme.

Theatre+ is a platform for long-term, collaborative creative work, designed to facilitate the exchange of ideas and showcase new dramaturgical and staging trends in contemporary theatre.

"The talented puppeteer Geppetto is a true artist! With love and skill, he crafts his dream son from a strange, playful piece of wood. He names him Pinocchio, and he turns out to be a character in his own right. A real ‘wooden head’ – headstrong, restless, curious and so naive that he cannot tell right from wrong.

Children are supposed to go to school, but Pinocchio simply won’t and won’t… He runs away and sets off on his difficult journey as a wandering wooden boy, getting into all sorts of trouble. Pinocchio longs to be a real boy and, through his adventures, discovers what it means to be alive. He realises the power of love. He experiences the magic of kindness. His guardian – the Blue-Haired Fairy – also reveals to him some unpleasant and shameful traits of character – such as lying. A faithful talking cricket accompanies him and advises him in times of danger, of which there are many.

The Wonderful Adventures of Pinocchio is a thrilling tale of ‘becoming human’, which the Italian writer Carlo Collodi told more than 140 years ago.

Did the mischievous Pinocchio become a real boy? Let’s experience his adventures together – AT THE THEATRE!

“The whole world is a stage and we are all actors – we enter, we exit, and in our own time each of us plays different roles. ”Man’s inability to find his true self is a theme I explored in Luigi Pirandello’s *Henry IV*. On the one hand, everyone sees you in their own way; on the other, you lose yourself behind the social masks you impose on yourself. In the constant shifting of one’s self-image, it becomes increasingly difficult to discover one’s true self.

The play *Because Mum Likes It That Way*, through an exaggerated, comedic lens, helps us realise that our pretence of a life distances us from our true selves – or from the life we long to have.

e3219387b24aa9594b14b7b58b6dd2b97d47e6e1.en:
INSERT COIN / PLAYER ONE is an electrifying, immersive performance that explores the blurred boundaries between the real and virtual worlds. The action unfolds within a surreal video game, where the audience becomes an active player in the struggle for identity, desire and control. Combining explosive choreography with intimate encounters with four characters, the production immerses the audience in a hyper-stylised world where the characters provoke, seduce and confuse them, vying for their attention. A hit with young audiences, the production pulsates with the energy of the present, where digital idols reign supreme, intimacy has been commodified, and contemporary dance becomes a personal and interactive experience.

At its core, INSERT COIN / PLAYER ONE is a game that you don’t just watch, but play in real time. By blurring the boundaries between performer and spectator, the performance draws the audience into a surreal, interactive space where every choice becomes choreography and every action alters the plot. The performance reminds us that the digital worlds we escape into are also mirrors, revealing the identities we construct.

The performance is an interactive, immersive experience in which the audience stands, with a limited number of seats available if required. The performance features strobe and flashing lights and is interactive, with dialogue between the performers and the audience.

e4e66b132c08db91d4360029fc7e56ea8efbb3c2.en:
*Chronicles of Pop-Folk* creates a theatrical space for that quasi-reality from which pop-folk emerged amidst the chaos of the 1990s. Pop-folk is not merely a musical genre. It is a manifesto of values, a philosophy of life, a cultural phenomenon which, in a way, has become a metaphor for post-socialist Bulgaria.

‘White Birds and Bullets’ is a theatrical chronicle, a scandalously candid account of the ‘golden’ years of pop-folk, spanning the period between the fall of the totalitarian regime and the downfall of the first leaders of organised crime – the patrons of this musical phenomenon, which later grew into the most successful sector of the Bulgarian show business industry.

e4e951d7f43be8352a300598ddebe493adc7a07f.en:
London in the 1920s. The wealthy Emily French is brutally murdered, and all the evidence points to Leonard Vole – a young charmer to whom the elderly lady had bequeathed her vast fortune. Accused of murder, Leonard is convinced that his partner – the enigmatic variety show dancer Romaine – can prove his innocence. But what happens when the defendant’s wife takes the stand?

‘Witness for the Prosecution’ is a play adapted by Agatha Christie from her 1925 short story ‘The Hands of the Traitor’, which has been the subject of numerous stage and film adaptations. Stoyan Radev – one of the most prominent directors on the Bulgarian theatre scene – takes on one of the most intriguing plots by the Queen of Crime, and together with the company of the Varna Drama Theatre, creates a production that grips the audience from start to finish.

e687828431b40b1af1911c691fb122951d4dbdf3.en:
For the second time, one of the most intriguing figures in European theatre, the Slovenian director Jernej Lorenci, will be staging a production with the National Theatre company. Following his production of *Orpheus*, Lorenzi returns to Sofia to work on Georgi Gospodinov’s novel *The Physics of Sorrow* (2012). The novel has been translated into more than 20 languages, won the prestigious international ‘Jan Michalski’ Prize in 2016 and was a finalist for the American PEN Translation Prize, the Premio Strega Europeo, the Haus der Kulturen der Welt Prize, the Gregor von Rezzori Prize and others. According to *The New Yorker*, ‘Georgi’s true quest in *The Physics of Sorrow* is to find a way to live with sorrow, to allow it to become a source of empathy and a beneficial fluctuation…’. The short animated film *The Physics of Sorrow*, based on the novel of the same name (dir. Teodor Ushev) has won numerous international awards and was shortlisted for the 2020 Oscars.

In the novel, time does not follow a chronological order, but is fragmentary, cyclical and experienced from within. ‘The Physics of Sorrow’ explores the way in which a person experiences time, history and loss through memory, empathy and stories. According to St Augustine’s understanding: time exists primarily in human consciousness, rather than as an objective flow. The past, present and future exist simultaneously; memory alters and bends time, whilst the present is fragile and fleeting.
